cd.headline: DR Congo presents FDLR disarmament progress at Egypt forum
cd.dek: Regional Integration Minister Floribert Anzuluni said two protocols cover disarmament, demobilisation and cantonment of FDLR fighters and affiliates.
paragraphs: DR Congo’s Regional Integration Minister Floribert Anzuluni presented progress on the voluntary surrender of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) fighters and affiliated organisations at the Aswan Forum in Egypt, according to a communiqué reported by Congo Independant on 24 November.

Anzuluni said two protocols had been signed covering disarmament, demobilisation and cantonment. He attended the forum’s sixth edition, which opened on 21 November, and joined a roundtable on durable peace in the Great Lakes region with Foreign Affairs Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba.

cd.headline: Opposition coalition backs Catholic leaders over religious restrictions
cd.dek: The Coalition Article 64 condemned a blocked Mass in Kinshasa and restrictions on Lubumbashi’s archbishop before a march over church land.
paragraphs: The Coalition Article 64, an opposition platform in DR Congo, voiced support on Tuesday, 24 November, for Catholic leaders and worshippers in Kinshasa and Lubumbashi after restrictions on religious activities and the repression of a march in Lubumbashi. The coalition criticised the cancellation of a Mass that Cardinal Fridolin Ambongo was due to lead with young Catholics at Tata Raphaël Stadium in Kinshasa.

C64 also said Lubumbashi Archbishop Fulgence Muteba was prevented from attending a peaceful march on 23 November. The archdiocese had organised the march to demand enforcement of a court decision concerning the Tshamalale site. Muteba also heads the National Episcopal Conference of Congo, the country’s Catholic bishops’ body.

In a statement, C64 said the measures extended restrictions into religious gatherings and raised concerns about public freedoms. Lubumbashi Mayor Joyce Tunda said the provincial government remained ready to continue dialogue with the church.

tz.headline: Nchemba urges electoral commissions to publish accurate information
tz.dek: Tanzania’s prime minister warned that information gaps let rumours spread and can weaken confidence in election bodies and the voting process.
paragraphs: Tanzania’s Prime Minister Mwigulu Nchemba urged Southern Africa’s electoral commissions to make accurate information readily available, saying gaps allow rumours to spread and risk dividing communities during elections. He spoke on November 23 in Dar es Salaam while opening the 28th annual conference of the Electoral Commissions Forum of SADC Countries, a two-day meeting on election management and social media.

Nchemba, representing President Samia Suluhu Hassan, said commissions should communicate reliably and prepare for artificial intelligence’s risks and opportunities. He said digital platforms are important information sources for young people and can support voter education, registration information and public participation, including among women, people with disabilities and pastoralist communities.

Justice Jacobs Mwambegele, chair of Tanzania’s electoral commission, said more than 108 participants from 15 commissions in 14 countries attended. Delegates were to exchange experience, develop common strategies and consider resolutions; the programme also included electing the forum’s leadership.

tz.headline: CHADEMA demands Lissu’s release before reconciliation talks
tz.dek: Deputy chair John Heche says the party will also require a mediator acceptable to both sides and talks on constitutional and electoral reforms.
paragraphs: Tanzania’s opposition party, the Chama cha Demokrasia na Maendeleo (CHADEMA), will not join President Samia Suluhu Hassan’s reconciliation process unless its imprisoned chairperson, Tundu Lissu, is freed unconditionally and an international mediator trusted by both sides takes part. Deputy chair John Heche set out the conditions at a press conference at the party’s headquarters in Mikocheni on November 24.

Heche said the central committee had reaffirmed the position at its August 29 meeting. Lissu should lead the party’s delegation, he said, and talks must address demands for a new constitution and electoral reforms. The party also wants other detained members freed, cases it calls fabricated withdrawn, and abductions ended.

Last week the High Court cleared Lissu of treason on November 6 but found him guilty of incitement and jailed him for four years. The judges said incitement was a lesser, related offence and that he had been able to defend himself, a finding he disputes.

tz.headline: Tanzania’s planning commission signs five-area pact with ODI Global
tz.dek: The UK-based organisation will work with the commission on research, development financing, monitoring and institutional capacity.
paragraphs: Tanzania’s National Planning Commission signed a memorandum of understanding with ODI Global, a UK-based international organisation, in Dar es Salaam to strengthen economic policymaking and planning for the country’s National Development Vision 2050.

Permanent Secretary Tausi Kida said the partnership covers five areas, including research on poverty, population growth, employment and livelihoods, and stronger monitoring and evaluation. The work is also intended to improve financing approaches, domestic resource mobilisation and the commission’s capacity in data analysis and economic modelling.

The partners also plan professional exchanges, joint research and academic platforms to build local expertise. Their work is intended to inform priorities in the Fourth Five-Year Development Plan and the Long-Term Perspective Plan.

tz.headline: Tanzania to hand CAF AFCON 2027 preparation offices
tz.dek: The handover is scheduled for November 25, 2026, in Dar es Salaam, alongside a sponsorship agreement between the tourism board and CAF.
paragraphs: Tanzania is scheduled to hand offices to the Confederation of African Football (CAF) on November 25, 2026, in Dar es Salaam, for use as the headquarters of preparations for AFCON 2027. The offices were built at the Julius Nyerere International Convention Centre, where the handover ceremony is due to begin at 3:00 a.m.

The ceremony will also include the signing of an advertising sponsorship agreement between the Ministry of Natural Resources and Tourism, through the Tanzania Tourist Board, and CAF. The agreement will make the board an official partner of the tournament.

Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda are jointly preparing to host AFCON 2027. The Ministry of Information, Culture, Arts and Sports has invited the public to follow the ceremony through media and social networks.

tz.headline: Tanzania and Cuba advance university research cooperation
tz.dek: Universities in both countries are implementing collaboration under agreements that include a 2023 framework between Dar es Salaam and Havana.
paragraphs: Tanzania and Cuba are advancing joint research and academic exchanges, with universities implementing areas of collaboration, Tanzania’s ambassador to Cuba, Lieutenant General Mathew Mkingule, said. He pointed to artificial intelligence, biotechnology, robotics and digital technologies as fields for closer work.

The countries signed two memoranda of understanding in September 2023, including one between the University of Dar es Salaam and the University of Havana. In January 2024, Tanzania’s Sokoine University of Agriculture signed a separate agreement with the University of Artemisa ‘Julio Díaz González’.

About 315 Tanzanian students had graduated from Cuban universities by 2020, including 209 medical personnel and 10 people trained in sports, Mkingule said. The Cuban government also built and donated three schools in Tanzania in the 1970s.

ma.headline: Moroccan tomato exports push European prices down to €1.10 per kilogram
ma.dek: Prices fell from €1.80 to €2 per kilogram as slower sales pressured traders to discount their produce.
paragraphs: Moroccan tomato exports to European markets have increased in recent weeks, cutting prices from €1.80 to €2 per kilogram to €1.10 to €1.30, according to a source at France’s Rungis International Market. The earlier range was equivalent to US$2.07 to US$2.30 per kilogram; the new range is US$1.27 to US$1.50.

Slower sales have squeezed traders’ expected profit margins, the source said, as some cut prices to avoid losses on perishable stock. More shipments are expected over the next two weeks as new crops ripen in Morocco’s Souss-Massa region.

French and Dutch tomatoes have remained available longer amid higher temperatures, increasing competition for Moroccan and Spanish supplies. Morocco’s Agriculture Minister Khalid Hatimi said authorities are tightening restrictions on exports to African markets until they assess domestic food needs.

ma.headline: Sports tribunal strips Morocco of 2025 Africa Cup title and awards it to Senegal
ma.dek: The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled unanimously, overturning the decision that had given Morocco the trophy on a forfeit.
paragraphs: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on Tuesday that Senegal won the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations, taking the title from Morocco. Morocco had been awarded the trophy on a forfeit.

ma.headline: Moroccan-origin groups press Spain parties for voter representation
ma.dek: The campaign comes as Vox calls for a review of naturalizations involving more than 300,000 Spanish citizens of Moroccan origin.
paragraphs: Moroccan-origin associations in Spain are urging parties to address their demands for political representation before the November 29 general election. On November 24, the Islamic Commission of Spain called on eligible Muslim voters to exercise their electoral rights and take part in decisions affecting Spanish society.

Commission president Aiman Adlbi said parliamentary decisions on government formation and public institutions affect Muslim citizens. Casa Marruecos held a gathering on November 15 in Quart de Poblet, near Valencia, to discuss racism, discrimination and political participation. Its vice-president, Boutaina El Hadri, said parties could no longer count on the community’s support without responding to its demands. She estimated that about 300,000 Spanish citizens of Moroccan origin were eligible to vote; the figure is not a confirmed electoral count.

The Socialist Party held an event for immigrant communities on November 24. El País reported that Vox wants to review naturalizations involving more than 300,000 Moroccan-origin citizens, but its report said the party’s programme does not establish wrongdoing in those cases.

ma.headline: Nexans Maroc opens innovation challenge applications through 31 December
ma.dek: The third edition sets four electrification challenges and accepts submissions from ideas to mature solutions.
paragraphs: Nexans Maroc has opened applications for the third Nexans Innovation Challenge, with submissions accepted from 23 November to 31 December 2026. The programme sets four industrial challenges under the theme of smarter, more sustainable and resilient electrification.

Nexans Maroc said the challenge is intended to connect industrial needs with solutions from startups, universities, research laboratories and entrepreneurs. Applicants can put forward an idea, prototype, pilot or more developed solution.

The company is running the initiative with Morocco’s industry and energy ministries, Mohammed VI Polytechnic University and the Renewable Energy Cluster. The challenges address electrification, including network digitalisation, renewable energy, artificial intelligence, decarbonisation, circular economy and infrastructure resilience.

ug.headline: Uganda urges banks to expand lending to women entrepreneurs
ug.dek: At a Kampala event, the central bank said 40% of women were in business, but only nine per cent had access to commercial loans.
paragraphs: Uganda urged financial institutions on Monday, November 23, to expand lending to women entrepreneurs and offer flexible financing, as it launched a data dashboard on women-owned small and medium enterprises in Kampala. Bank of Uganda Deputy Governor Augustus Nuwagaba said about 40% of women were engaged in business, but only 18% could access loans and nine per cent commercial loans.

Nuwagaba called for financing that recognises group collateral, allowing women to borrow collectively. He cited the central bank’s Agricultural Credit Facility and Small Business Fund, which offers loans at an interest rate of 10%. Sarah Kagingo, vice chair of the Private Sector Foundation Uganda board, urged lenders to tailor products to women-owned businesses rather than apply uniform conditions.

Kagingo said 77.2% of women-led businesses that accessed financing through the GROW Project reported increased household incomes in less than two years. She added that formalisation among participating businesses rose from 17.4% to 42%.

ug.headline: Kiira Motors builds Uganda’s vehicle industry from a university prototype
ug.dek: The company’s Jinja plant is designed to produce up to 5,000 vehicles a year as it advances electric buses and regional-market plans.
paragraphs: President Yoweri Museveni launched Uganda’s first homegrown electric vehicle, the two-seat Kiira EV, at Makerere University on November 24, 2011. Students and staff developed the battery-powered prototype through the university’s Centre for Research in Transportation Technologies.

The vehicle was a proof of concept, not a commercial model. Kiira Motors Corporation was established in 2014 as a state enterprise jointly owned by the Ugandan government and Makerere University. Its Jinja plant, in the Jinja Industrial and Business Park, is designed for annual output of up to 5,000 vehicles, with shops for bodywork, paint, chassis, trim and final assembly.

The company has moved towards commercial production with its Kayoola electric buses and has outlined plans to expand their use in Ugandan cities and pursue regional markets. It also plans to raise local content, develop domestic suppliers and explore battery manufacturing.

ug.headline: Museveni appoints Nawangwe to lead higher education regulator
ug.dek: The National Council for Higher Education had gone months without a substantive chair, delaying some decisions requiring the full council.
paragraphs: President Yoweri Museveni appointed Makerere University Vice-Chancellor Prof Barnabas Nawangwe chairperson of Uganda’s National Council for Higher Education (NCHE), the regulator for higher education, in an instrument signed on November 14. Nawangwe replaces Prof Joy Constance Kyesiga, who left the role after retiring as Kabale University vice-chancellor.

Sources at the Ministry of Education and Sports and NCHE confirmed the appointment to Uganda Radio Network. The council’s leadership gap delayed some strategic policy decisions, approvals and regulatory determinations requiring full council participation, while routine regulatory work continued under its executive director and staff.

Nawangwe’s appointment provides for five years, but his final term as Makerere vice-chancellor ends in August 2027. His predecessor also left the chair after retiring from a public university leadership role.

ug.headline: Tayebwa backs UWA’s expanded forest role and seeks resources
ug.dek: The deputy speaker pledged Parliament’s support as the wildlife authority takes over central forest reserves and seeks a helicopter for its operations.
paragraphs: Uganda’s Deputy Speaker, Thomas Tayebwa, pledged Parliament’s continued support for the Uganda Wildlife Authority (UWA) on November 24, 2026, as it takes on management of central forest reserves. He met UWA Executive Director James Musinguzi at Parliament.

Musinguzi asked Tayebwa to help secure a helicopter for aerial surveillance, wildlife protection and emergency response, and said UWA needed more funding for its expanded duties. Tayebwa said the authority’s performance had informed Parliament’s support for adding the forests to its responsibilities.

Tayebwa also pledged to mobilise colleagues for a rhino-naming ceremony scheduled for January 16, 2027, and urged UWA to habituate more chimpanzee groups in Maramagambo Forest to expand tracking tourism. He committed to supporting tourism initiatives, particularly chimpanzee tourism.

ug.headline: Stellenbosch selects Uganda’s Winnie Byanyima for honorary commerce doctorate
ug.dek: The university named the outgoing UNAIDS chief among seven recipients, citing her work on social justice, women’s rights and global inequality.
paragraphs: Stellenbosch University in South Africa has selected Winnie Byanyima, Uganda’s outgoing Executive Director of the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), for an honorary Doctor of Commerce. The university named her among seven recipients of honorary degrees.

Byanyima, an engineer and United Nations Under-Secretary-General, served three terms in Uganda’s Parliament and founded the Forum for Women in Democracy, which promotes women’s leadership. She also held senior roles at the African Union Commission, the United Nations Development Programme and Oxfam International before taking the UNAIDS post in 2019.

Her previous honorary degrees came from the University of Manchester, Mount Saint Vincent University in Canada, Cranfield University and the University of the Free State in South Africa. The other recipients include Nigerian journalist Dele Olojede and retired South African judge Dennis Davis.

zw.headline: Zimbabwe drought puts at least 40% of cattle herd at risk
zw.dek: A Cabinet update links the El Niño drought to pressure on farmers, while Treasury projects growth will slow to 1.2% in 2027.
paragraphs: Cabinet has warned that at least 40% of Zimbabwe's cattle herd is exposed to the El Niño-driven drought, a risk it says could bring significant livestock losses. Cattle farmers are already under strain, and some are selling off their animals.
Livestock sits among the agricultural value chains the update flags as facing heightened exposure. The worsening conditions add pressure to farm output more broadly.
Treasury's latest projections put growth at 1.2% in 2027, down from 5% this year, with the slowdown tied largely to El Niño and other global shocks.

zw.headline: South Africa deports Zimbabwean after suspended sentence over Ukraine plans
zw.dek: Wesley Sothole, 24, pleaded guilty to planning to travel to Ukraine; four other Zimbabweans arrested with him have yet to enter pleas.
paragraphs: South Africa deported Wesley Sothole, a 24-year-old Zimbabwean, after a court handed him a five-year suspended prison sentence for planning to fight in the Russia-Ukraine war. He pleaded guilty at Kempton Park Magistrates' Court.

South African media reports said Sothole was one of five Zimbabweans arrested at OR Tambo International Airport in Johannesburg on November 8. Prosecutors have not said which side the group allegedly planned to fight for.

Court dates now fall to the other four, whose case returns to Kempton Park on December 1. Since the start of this year, a Ukrainian intelligence assessment has put the number of Africans recruited to fight for Russia at more than 1 700, from 36 countries.

zw.headline: Highlanders end strike and commit to two fixtures
zw.dek: The players had refused to travel for a league match amid unpaid salaries, bonuses and allowances; the club says the union accepted its offer.
paragraphs: Highlanders have reached an agreement with the Footballers’ Union of Zimbabwe (FUZ) to fulfil two fixtures this week, ending a players’ strike over unpaid salaries, bonuses and allowances. The club’s executive committee announced the deal on Tuesday, 24 November, after discussions with the union and the Premier Soccer League (PSL) on Sunday.

The players had refused to travel to Wadzanai Stadium for the scheduled Saturday, 21 November, league match against Agama. Highlanders said FUZ accepted the club’s offer and would help ensure the fixtures go ahead. The rescheduled league match against Agama is set for Wadzanai Stadium at 2 pm on Wednesday, 25 November.

Highlanders are also scheduled to play Hardrock in the Chibuku Super Cup final at Chahwanda Stadium in Kwekwe on Saturday. The PSL also rescheduled Herentals College’s match against ZPC Kariba, with both league games set to kick off at 2 pm.

zw.headline: Air Zimbabwe reschedules London flights to 26 and 27 November
zw.dek: The carrier says the London-to-Harare service will resume on 26 November after a flight was rescheduled, while the Harare-to-London flight moves to 27 November.
paragraphs: Air Zimbabwe said its London-to-Harare flight will resume on 26 November, after a service scheduled for 23 November was rescheduled for operational reasons. The Harare-to-London flight, originally set for 25 November, will now operate on 27 November, the airline said in an update issued on 24 November.

Plus Ultra Líneas Aéreas, the Spanish carrier that supplies the aircraft and crew under a wet lease, suspended all flight operations on 23 November until further notice, grounding its last scheduled service between Spain and Caracas. Air Zimbabwe sells tickets and manages the route commercially, while Plus Ultra provides the aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance. The route uses a 302-seat Airbus A330-300.

Air Zimbabwe restarted direct Harare-London flights on 22 July 2026, ending a 14-year absence from the route. The service links Harare's Robert Gabriel Mugabe International Airport with London Gatwick's South Terminal.

cv.headline: Cape Verde’s CVsky carries 306 medical evacuation passengers
cv.dek: The airline has taken over a service among the Coast Guard King Air’s planned missions since the aircraft’s operation was suspended.
paragraphs: Cape Verde’s CVsky has carried 306 passengers on medical evacuations since 29 March, taking over a service among the planned missions of the Coast Guard’s King Air aircraft. The government suspended the plane’s operation.

Colonel Domingos Correia, who previously led the military aviation project, told Expresso das Ilhas that the suspension reduced the country’s capacity for medical evacuations and maritime security. He said the aircraft was designed for several duties, including transporting patients, and disputed the government’s economic justification for stopping its use.
The King Air’s suspension has prompted debate over how Cape Verde provides medical evacuations, while CVsky continues to carry patients.

cv.headline: Praia water company dismantles more than 100 illegal connections
cv.dek: Águas de Santiago says some connections supplied water for resale, crop irrigation and construction, while others bypassed meters or followed debt suspensions.
paragraphs: Águas de Santiago, the company responsible for water supply in Santiago, has dismantled more than 100 illegal connections in Praia over the past three months, it said. The work is part of inspections aimed at irregularities in the public water system.

The company said some connections were used to sell water to third parties, irrigate vegetable plots on the city’s outskirts or supply construction sites, housing complexes and rental buildings. Other methods included reconnecting service after suspension for unpaid bills, tapping the network without a meter, removing meters and using bypass devices.

Águas de Santiago said the practices increase water losses and affect the sustainability and fairness of the service. It did not provide a figure for the water lost or set out a date for further inspections.

cv.dek: The composer and former member of Voz de Cabo Verde wrote “Crioulo na França,” a song associated with emigration and ties to the diaspora.
paragraphs: Joaquim Soares de Almeida, the Cabo Verdean musician known as Morgadinho, died in Paris at 95, his family announced. A composer, singer and instrumentalist, he was a member of Voz de Cabo Verde in its first formation.

cv.headline: Cape Verde French teachers test new classroom methods
cv.dek: A two-day colloquium in Mindelo brought 70 teachers together to share approaches to grammar, digital tools and teaching children.
paragraphs: A two-day national colloquium for French teachers from São Vicente and Santo Antão ended on 24 November at the Mindelo Technology Park, with 70 teachers attending. The event focused on teaching methods, classroom tools and ways to make French lessons more engaging.

Maria Helena dos Santos, a trainer and São Vicente representative of the Cape Verde Association of French Teachers, said the training was intended to equip teachers for changing demands in foreign-language education. Participants took part in four workshops on topics including teaching French to children, digital tools, the TV5MONDE platform, a French-language television network, and more interactive grammar lessons.

The association organised the colloquium with the French Embassy. It followed a July training in France attended by 16 teachers from different islands, who were expected to share what they learned with colleagues. Dos Santos said students have few opportunities to encounter French outside class.

td.headline: Chad allocates CFA420 billion and 90 billion in external funds to roads
td.dek: The 2027 budget sets total investment at 1 458,132 milliards de FCFA, up 24%, with roads taking more than 53% of domestic investment resources.
paragraphs: Chad’s parliament approved a 2027 budget on Tuesday that allocates 420 milliards de FCFA from domestic resources and 90 milliards of external financing exclusively to road infrastructure. Total investment spending is set at 1 458,132 milliards de FCFA, a 24% increase.

The parliamentary report says the road programme is intended to link production areas with markets and improve movement of people and goods. Investment financed from the state’s own resources totals 795,5 milliards de FCFA, compared with 618 milliards in 2026; externally financed investment is 662,6 milliards.

The government’s plan, Tchad Connexion 2030, puts infrastructure at the centre of development. Technical and financial partners will scrutinise whether local companies and the administration can execute the investment budget within one calendar year.

paragraphs: Chad’s National Assembly adopted the 2027 budget on Tuesday, raising allocations to autonomous local authorities to CFA58 billion from CFA47 billion in 2026. The increase is part of a CFA344.9 billion transfers and subsidies budget line, up 13%.

td.headline: Niger's Tiani summons advisory council after Chad protests expulsions
td.dek: The council is due to meet on 1 December as Chad condemns the collective expulsion of Mahamid civilians and calls for case-by-case review.
paragraphs: Niger's President Abdourahamane Tiani has called the Council consultatif de la refondation to meet on 1 December 2026, after Chad protested Niger's expulsion of Mahamid citizens. A decree summons the council, according to a statement from Niger's government secretariat.

Gassim Cherif Mahamat, Chad's government spokesman, called the collective expulsions a breach of international commitments and said they risk creating stateless people. He said Chad rejects Niger's security justification and plans to examine cases individually. The spokesman cited Article 12(5) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, which prohibits collective expulsions.

Chad's government urged its people to show solidarity with those arriving in the country while it seeks clarification from Niger's authorities. It also called on partners to press Niger to respect international law.

dj.headline: Djibouti and Madagascar set joint port committee as condition for maritime cooperation
dj.dek: President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh proposed exchanges on port management, training and digital logistics, as well as transport and cargo-handling infrastructure.
paragraphs: Djibouti and Madagascar agreed to establish a joint port committee as a condition for pursuing maritime cooperation, Djibouti's President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh said during a meeting with Madagascar's President Michaël Randrianirina. Guelleh proposed exchanges on port management, training, digital logistics operations and transport and cargo-handling infrastructure.

Guelleh cited existing maritime ties, including the Djibouti Code of Conduct, a regional agreement against piracy adopted in 2009 under the International Maritime Organization, and a regional maritime information-fusion centre based in Madagascar that monitors traffic in the western Indian Ocean. Madagascar's delegation included Hertiana Randriamâhoaka, director general of Toamasina port, the island's main port.

Guelleh also proposed that the two countries coordinate their participation in international carbon markets. Randrianirina said agreements signed during his visit would give the trip concrete content.

sz.headline: Eswatini PM demands deadlines and consequences for underperforming officials
sz.dek: Russell Dlamini said supervisors must investigate poor performance and allow time to improve, as delayed budget releases hinder ministries.
paragraphs: Eswatini Prime Minister Russell Dlamini told ministers and principal secretaries at a government performance review in Ezulwini that persistently underperforming public officers should face disciplinary consequences under public service rules.

The review found that delays and shortfalls in releasing approved funds had compromised service delivery. Dlamini said supervisors should establish why an officer was performing poorly, provide support where needed and set a timetable for improvement; he did not specify sanctions. He also called for each priority government commitment to have a responsible officer, a deadline and a measurable result.
Government scored 48% for the 2025/26 financial year, up from 22% in its first quarter, but faced procurement bottlenecks, legislative delays and weaknesses in project planning.

sz.headline: Eswatini to roll out maths and science initiatives in 160 schools
sz.dek: The education ministry is expanding the programmes nationwide to make lessons more interactive and address weak performance in the two subjects.
paragraphs: Eswatini’s Ministry of Education and Training will expand its Progressive Mathematics Initiative and Progressive Science Initiative to 160 secondary and high schools across all four regions. The programmes are intended to replace chalkboard-led teaching with interactive classroom lessons.

Chief Inspector of Secondary Education Phumlile Dlamini announced the expansion at a sensitisation workshop in Manzini. She said examination data and education-sector analyses showed persistent poor performance in foundational and junior secondary Mathematics and Science. Head teachers and school committee chairpersons from Lubombo and Manzini attended to prepare for their implementation responsibilities.

The initiative is part of a World Bank-funded project to strengthen basic education and human-capital development in Eswatini. The ministry says the new approach is intended to build learners’ confidence and interest in the subjects.

sz.headline: Eswatini tourism authority urges 228 accommodation businesses to report online
sz.dek: The authority says the sector grew from 165 establishments in 2019, but better occupancy and guest data are needed to guide policy and investment.
paragraphs: Eswatini’s accommodation sector grew from 165 establishments in 2019 to 228 in 2026, and the Eswatini Tourism Authority is urging operators to submit monthly business data online. The Central Statistical Office introduced the platform in collaboration with the authority, replacing paper questionnaires.

Authority chief executive Vusie Dlamini said operators should make online submissions part of their normal business routines and ensure staff understand the reporting requirements. He said figures on room occupancy, guest numbers, length of stay and facility use help assess the sector’s performance and guide government policy and private investment.

National economic statistics put tourism’s contribution to gross domestic product at 1.4% in 2025; accommodation and food services accounted for 0.8% of that contribution. Dlamini said those figures cover direct activity, not tourism’s full value across other sectors.

sz.headline: Simelane runs 120km to support Eswatini renal patients
sz.dek: The Royal Eswatini Sugar employee finished a solo route from Siteki to Lavumisa in under 24 hours, with funds raised still to be tallied.
paragraphs: Andreas Simelane, an ultra-marathon runner and Royal Eswatini Sugar Corporation employee, completed a 120km solo run from Siteki to Lavumisa on Tuesday to raise awareness for men’s health. He finished at about 6pm, in under 24 hours, despite adverse weather.

The initiative, run with the Ministry of Health, will benefit the Renal Association Eswatini. Simelane said he wanted to give hope to the association’s 300 patients. Several corporate sponsors have backed the drive, and organisers have left it open to further partners before announcing the final fundraising total.

The run doubled the 60km distance set by the annual Move for Movember challenge, which encourages participants to cover 60km during November. Simelane also completed a 161km race in South Africa in August and a 109km solo run the following month.

ga.headline: Gabon's mining transparency body warns of suspension without 2024 report
ga.dek: An administration group took its campaign to Étéké, where residents raised concerns about environmental damage and limited development.
paragraphs: Gabon's administration group for the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (ITIE-Gabon) held meetings in Étéké, in the Ngounié province, from 23 to 24 October to explain the transparency standard and discuss small-scale artisanal mining. The country risks another suspension from the initiative if it does not publish its 2024 report by 31 December 2026.

Patricia Oussou, the group's focal point, led the delegation. The standard requires states and extractive companies to report production, exports, revenue and how proceeds are allocated. Residents raised concerns about environmental damage from earlier mining, Étéké's limited development despite its gold potential and miners' difficulty reaching extraction sites.
Gabon rejoined the initiative in 2021 and scored 73.5 points in March 2025. A group member warned that missing the year-end deadline would lead to another expulsion.

ga.headline: Gabon university leaders discuss aligning courses and recognising degrees
ga.dek: The fifth rectors’ conference opened in Libreville with talks on shared resources and making qualifications easier to recognise across Gabon and the CEMAC region.
paragraphs: Gabon’s fifth conference of university rectors, leaders of major schools and research institutions opened on 23 November at Omar Bongo University in Libreville. Participants are discussing ways to align courses, improve recognition of degrees and share resources across institutions.

The talks bring education leaders together with their supervising authorities to address problems affecting the national training system, Gabon Review reported. Discussions include aligning course plans and programmes to make qualifications easier to recognise and circulate nationally, across the Central African Economic and Monetary Community (CEMAC) and internationally.

Participants also raised sharing staff, equipment and technical facilities to improve training and strengthen scientific research. The conference has not announced reforms; its proposals would need to be turned into concrete changes.

ga.headline: GDJ and football league sign 2026-2029 sponsorship deal
ga.dek: The agreement covers Gabon’s first and second divisions, with clubs urged to build their own income and include women’s football.
paragraphs: Gabonese gaming company Gabonaise des Jeux (GDJ) and the National Professional Football League signed a sponsorship agreement in Libreville on 23 November, covering the 2026-2029 seasons. It supports the country’s first- and second-division championships.

League president Brice Mbika said the deal is intended to improve competition organisation and support clubs. Sports Minister Paul Ulrich Kessany said clubs benefiting from the agreement must develop their own revenue to remain viable, and urged them to strengthen lower-age categories and women’s football.

GDJ marketing and communications director Stéphane Nwa said the partnership backs more sustainable organisation and a return of supporters to stadiums. The agreement’s stated goals also include strengthening clubs and improving the experience of people involved in Gabonese football.

ga.headline: Gabon writers’ union president joins Benin book fair
ga.dek: Éric Joël Békalé took part in the four-day Cotonou gathering, where writers discussed African poetry, memory and writing in African languages.
paragraphs: Éric Joël Békalé, president of Gabon’s writers’ union, attended the fifth National Book Fair of Benin in Cotonou from 19 to 22 November 2026. The event’s theme was “Poetry in all its forms.” Békalé joined authors from Togo, Congo, Cameroon, Haiti, Mauritania and Mali.

The four-day fair brought together writers, literary critics, teachers, journalists and readers for discussions on the renewal of African poetry, links between slam and poetry, and writing in African languages. Its opening conference asked whether poetry could help address contemporary challenges. Writer Roger Sidokpohou spoke about preserving individual and collective memories and called for a renewed role for the griot in passing on knowledge, myths, rituals and values.
The programme also included writing workshops for young people and children. Florent Couao-Zotti, the fair’s general delegate, said poetry could go beyond artistic expression.

gm.headline: Bensouda proposes tariffs to curb D500 million in furniture imports
gm.dek: The Gambian presidential candidate says government procurement alone accounts for about D100 million of the imported furniture bill.
paragraphs: Talib Ahmed Bensouda, the Unite Movement for Change presidential candidate, has proposed using import duties and tariffs to curb imports of products that can be made locally, citing about D500 million spent on imported furniture in The Gambia. He made the proposal in an interview during his campaign tour of the provinces.

Bensouda said government procurement accounts for about D100 million of that furniture, all of it imported. He argued that local timber could support furniture manufacturing and jobs, and said his economic policy would prioritise domestic production and investment in local industries.

His 66-point agenda also proposes an agricultural bank and a small finance bank for farmers, horticultural producers and people raising animals. He pledged a minimum-wage policy covering public and private sector workers and proposed removing ceilings on groundnut prices.

gm.headline: Gambia contempt dispute tests limits on court powers
gm.dek: A reporter says she was threatened with prison after an exchange at the High Court; the judiciary and prison service had not responded.
paragraphs: A court reporter in The Gambia says she was threatened with committal to Mile 2 Prison after an exchange at the High Court, according to a report published by The Alkamba Times on November 23, 2026. The reporter had covered proceedings, left the courtroom and photographed an accused person within the court complex.

The report says a prison officer allegedly tried to take her phone and that the reporter was accused of using foul language. It says she was not given an opportunity to explain herself. The Alkamba Times said its account was one side of the dispute; the judiciary and prison service had not responded.

Section 122 of the Constitution gives superior courts contempt powers. Section 99 allows summary conviction for listed offences only when committed in the face of the court; conduct outside it calls for a charge and a hearing, according to the article.

gm.headline: Barrow predicts victory in Fulladu on December 5
gm.dek: The Gambian president said his administration strengthened democracy and cited roads, boreholes, electricity, schools and hospitals in his re-election pitch.
paragraphs: President Adama Barrow said he expects to win in Fulladu in The Gambia’s December 5 presidential election, speaking at a campaign meeting in Taifa, Central River Region. He said his administration’s democratic reforms had made it easier for opponents to challenge him, but argued they would not win enough support in Fulladu.

Barrow described the presidency as a five-year contract with voters and said an incumbent must return to them to account for his record. He cited roads, boreholes, expanded electricity access, schools, hospitals, community ambulances and support for agriculture as evidence of his government’s work.

At rallies elsewhere in Central River Region South, supporters praised development projects and pledged backing for another term. Barrow said larger projects would begin in 2027 and that contracts had been signed to extend electricity to villages not yet connected to the national grid.

gm.headline: Jallow welcomes ruling in Gambia's Rohingya case against Myanmar
gm.dek: The retired chief justice says the judgment on Myanmar's treatment of Rohingya people sets a precedent for state responsibility.
paragraphs: Retired Gambian Chief Justice Hassan B. Jallow has welcomed a judgment by the International Court of Justice in The Hague in the case The Gambia brought against Myanmar over the treatment of the Rohingya people. The ruling was delivered last week, The Point reported.

Jallow, a former chief prosecutor at the United Nations Rwanda Tribunal and the UN Mechanism for International Criminal Tribunals, called the judgment an important milestone in international criminal justice. He said earlier UN ad hoc tribunals and some national courts had held individuals to account for serious rights violations, and that the ruling sets an excellent precedent for state responsibility.

Jallow commended the government under President Adama Barrow for initiating and pursuing the case, and the Ministry of Justice under successive attorneys general Baa Tambadou and Dawda A. Jallow for managing it. He described the case as another instance of The Gambia's long-standing commitment to human rights protection.

gm.headline: Fye Network and Booksmarte launch campaign to distribute 10,000 books
gm.dek: The Gambian partners will begin with the Q Read Initiative, targeting children across all seven regions through book distribution and reading activities.
paragraphs: Fye Network, a Gambian-founded creative media company, and Booksmarte, a local education organization, have partnered on a nationwide literacy campaign. Their Q Read Initiative seeks to place 10,000 books in children’s hands and reach 10,000 young Gambians through book distribution and community reading activities.

Under the agreement, Fye Network will provide children’s publishing, storytelling and creative content, while Booksmarte will coordinate locally, engage communities and schools, and deliver the campaign nationwide. The partners plan reading programs, storytelling sessions and educational events with schools, educators, families and communities.

The organizations are seeking sponsorships and other contributions from individuals, businesses, institutions and development partners. They also plan further reading programs, school activities and community events beyond Q Read.

gn.headline: Guinea presents sovereign fund bill to lawmakers
gn.dek: The proposal would require National Assembly approval for withdrawals and sets out rules for managing mining revenues.
paragraphs: Guinea’s government presented a bill to create and govern a sovereign wealth fund to a special joint committee of the National Assembly on Monday, 23 November 2026. Economy, Finance and Budget Minister Mariama Ciré Sylla led the presentation, joined by the government secretary-general and the minister responsible for international cooperation.

Sylla said the fund would not operate as a parallel budget or borrow money. Any withdrawal would require prior approval from the National Assembly, and the proposed governance framework draws on the Santiago Principles for sovereign funds. The Assembly’s Laws Committee recommended strengthening the legal framework, transparency and safeguards for national resources.

The government answered lawmakers’ concerns and accepted several proposals. The fund is intended to convert non-renewable mining resources into lasting assets, with development financing, economic stabilisation and intergenerational equity as its three pillars.

paragraphs: A Guinean court’s investigating chamber issued a non-indictment order for Zenab Dramé, a former minister of technical education and vocational training, on September 30 in the Nabayagate case. The allegations concerned the alleged misappropriation of more than 200 billion Guinean francs.

Dramé’s lawyers announced the ruling in a statement released on Wednesday, November 25, and said they were reserving the right to bring legal action against people they accuse of defamation and false denunciation. They also cited a November 12 television appearance by the special prosecutor, who they said publicly acknowledged a lack of factual evidence supporting the accusations made through the press.

gn.headline: Guinea’s government sets out results-focused approach after retreat
gn.dek: Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah says ministries will coordinate projects, track delivery and settle cross-government issues at senior level.
paragraphs: Guinea’s government has set out a plan to coordinate ministries, monitor projects and make senior-level decisions after a three-day retreat in Forécariah that ended Tuesday. Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah said the approach would replace departments working in separate silos with shared responsibility for government decisions.

Bah said ministries had seen during the discussions that their success depended on colleagues’ actions and on preparing projects with the bodies responsible for monitoring them. He said issues previously handled by individual administrations were compared, ranked and directed towards resolution, with the state expected to prepare before making commitments.

The government also presented its approach as a guide for Guinea’s Simandou 2040 horizon. The report said the retreat covered instruments for project monitoring, budget accountability and senior-level arbitration; it gave no further details of their timetable.

gn.headline: Guinea champions FireBall qualify for 2026 African women’s club finals
gn.dek: The club earned its place after winning Guinea’s championship, with no zonal qualifying tournament held this season.
paragraphs: FireBall Athletic Club, the Guinea women’s basketball champion, has qualified for the final phase of the Women’s Basketball League Africa (WBLA) 2026. The tournament is scheduled for Cairo, Egypt, from 11 to 20 December.

The club’s executive board announced the qualification in a statement shared on social media. With no zonal qualifying tournament this season, FireBall’s national title secured its place. The club is the first Guinean women’s team to reach this stage of the African competition.
The players will face teams from across Africa in Cairo, where club officials say logistical and sporting challenges await.

gw.headline: Dias demands publication of Guinea-Bissau election results
gw.dek: The former presidential candidate says he has his own voting data and claims he won the November 2025 ballot, which was interrupted by a coup.
paragraphs: Fernando Dias da Costa, a former presidential candidate in Guinea-Bissau, demanded publication of results from the November 23, 2025, election, which was interrupted by a coup. Speaking on Tuesday during a visit to the political movement Seco Bari, which backed his candidacy, Dias said he had his own data from the vote and claimed he received the most votes.

Dias said the results should be announced because, in his view, there was no obstacle to doing so. He also said he and the PAI-Terra Ranka coalition had chosen reconciliation, and said they forgave those involved in how they were treated during the election process.
The visit followed a partial easing of restrictions on political activity by the High Military Command. Dias called on Guineans to pursue dialogue, tolerance and inclusion.

gw.headline: Guinea-Bissau's PRS urges dialogue to end transition and hold elections
gw.dek: The party says a calm political climate is needed before the military command decides when the transition will end and elections will be held.
paragraphs: Guinea-Bissau’s Social Renewal Party (PRS) urged national parties and political actors on Tuesday, 24 November, to pursue dialogue and agreement, saying this could help create conditions to end the transition and hold free, fair and transparent elections.

The appeal was read at the party’s national headquarters in Santa Luzia, Bissau, by communications coordinator Francelino Cunha. The PRS said the military command’s partial easing of restrictions showed sensitivity to people’s wish for peace and full civic and political rights. It also told its national, regional and sectoral structures, members and leaders to observe the authorities’ rules and keep political activity peaceful, organised and lawful.

The military command will decide on completing the transition and setting an election date, the party said. The PRS also reported that preparations for its congress were progressing satisfactorily and urged members to take part in an active and disciplined way.

lr.headline: Boakai to sign US$5.7 billion Bea Mountain power and roads deal
lr.dek: The plan promises 270 MW of new generation, US$230 million for the grid and a 146 km road, with lawmakers next to decide whether to ratify it.
paragraphs: Liberian President Joseph Nyuma Boakai is due to sign a US$5.7 billion infrastructure agreement with Bea Mountain Mining Corporation on Wednesday. The Legislature must ratify the deal after his signature. The plan would add 270 MW of power through four plants and fund a 146 km road linking the plants to key facilities.

The government says it will finance the work by setting aside additional revenue payable by the mining company, rather than taking new loans. Bea Mountain is also pledging US$500 million in bridge financing while continuing its regular payments to the Consolidated Account. The package includes US$230 million to upgrade substations, transformers and transmission lines.

The government says the program would take five years, with the biomass plant and transmission lines targeted within two years. Critics have warned that the terms could give the company too much of Liberia’s future gold income; the most detailed objection cited in the report came from Rev. Dr. Samuel B. Reeves Jr., president of the Liberia Council of Churches.

lr.headline: Liberia task force alleges US$1.2 billion in annual gold smuggling
lr.dek: PORT chairman Abraham Kromah says gold leaves the country outside tax collection, while residents demand records of recoveries and prosecutions.
paragraphs: Abraham Kromah, chairman of Liberia’s Protect Our Resources Task Force (PORT), alleged that about US$1.2 billion worth of gold is smuggled out of Liberia each year. He made the claim during a local radio appearance in Monrovia over the weekend, saying the gold bypasses the Liberia Revenue Authority.

Kromah said PORT had identified people allegedly financing and facilitating illegal mining and warned they would face prosecution. He also alleged links between illegal mining and drug cartels, and said the task force was working with the Liberia Immigration Service on immigration violations, including deportation where legally justified. The claims, including the smuggling estimate and criminal links, require independent verification.

Residents in Gbarpolu County are questioning why mineral-rich communities remain poor and lack adequate public services. Citizens are seeking figures on gold and diamonds recovered, equipment seized, suspects arrested, cases prosecuted and revenue returned to government.

lr.headline: Liberia's justice ministry plans legal redress after split jury in child rape trial
lr.dek: Eight jurors voted to acquit Patrick Weefur and four to convict, leaving a case involving a 13-year-old girl without a verdict.
paragraphs: A split jury at Criminal Court E at the Temple of Justice in Monrovia returned a hung verdict in the rape case against Patrick Weefur, producing a mistrial. Eight jurors voted to acquit him and four to convict.

Cllr. Isaac L. George, director of the Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Crimes Unit at the Ministry of Justice, said prosecutors were troubled that Weefur had sought to change his not-guilty plea to guilty after the government had called about five witnesses, including the alleged victim. Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh declined to accept the guilty plea under Chapter 16.4 of Liberia's Criminal Procedure Law, but allowed Weefur to waive his right to testify.
The unit said it plans to pursue legal redress over the jury's handling of the case.

lr.headline: Monrovia mayor-designate proposes US$14.5 million city plan
lr.dek: James K. Mulbah’s six-part agenda includes a digital revenue registry, waste collection zones and a drainage programme with the public works ministry.
paragraphs: Monrovia Mayor-designate James K. Mulbah presented a proposed US$14.5 million development plan at a confirmation hearing before the Liberian Senate Committee on Local Government. Its six pillars cover municipal revenue, waste management, urban beautification, drainage and climate resilience, stakeholder coordination and climate financing.

Mulbah proposed a Digital Monrovia Revenue Registry to register properties and businesses, assign them municipal identification numbers and improve billing and collection. His sanitation plan would divide the city into waste zones and pay contractors according to verified performance; a “Separate Your Waste” pilot would begin in Sinkor.

He also proposed planting 200,000 indigenous, climate-resilient trees and working with the Ministry of Public Works on drainage mapping, routine cleaning and waste control. The plan includes green corridors along Tubman Boulevard and Somalia Drive.

lr.headline: Liberian-founded IT firm KaynTech weighs expansion into Liberia
lr.dek: The Minneapolis company, set up about a year ago by Kromah Alhaji, sells IT services to U.S. businesses and may later open jobs in Liberia.
paragraphs: A Minneapolis information technology company founded by Liberian Kromah Alhaji is preparing a possible expansion into Liberia. KaynTech Solutions LLC was established about a year ago and offers its services to businesses across the United States.

Alhaji, who is co-founder and chief executive, describes the firm's work as reaching from IT consulting to cloud computing, infrastructure management, database solutions and technology integration. No date has been set for a Liberian expansion, and the company has not given a figure for the employment it could create.

Alhaji also works as a senior cloud infrastructure engineer for the Minnesota State Colleges and Universities system. Earlier, while at the University of Liberia, he was elected student representative to the Faculty Senate.

ly.headline: US renews call for unified Libyan government and credible elections
ly.dek: Spokesman Tommy Pigott said Washington backs an inclusive, Libyan-led process as Libya’s parliament announced a separate roadmap initiative.
paragraphs: The US Department of State renewed its call on Tuesday for Libya to form a unified government able to control the country’s territory and hold transparent, credible national elections. Spokesman Tommy Pigott said Washington wants a unified executive authority.

Pigott said integrating Libya’s political, economic and security institutions is central to lasting stability. He also said the United States supports initiatives for an inclusive political process led by Libyans and based on national consensus.

Libya’s House of Representatives announced a new roadmap initiative on Tuesday to unify state institutions and renew legitimacy through elections. Earlier this week, a delegation from the Tripoli-based government met US officials in Washington to discuss energy-sector economic and trade partnerships.

ly.headline: Menfi seeks settlement with Misurata and Zintan leaders to enable elections

paragraphs: Mohamed al-Menfi, chairman of Libya’s Presidential Council, met community elders and local dignitaries from Misurata and Zintan in Tripoli on Monday to discuss a settlement that could enable presidential and parliamentary elections.

Menfi called for a Libyan-led process with broad participation and no segment of society excluded. The delegation backed his efforts to build national consensus and preserve the country’s unity and sovereignty.
The talks also addressed ending successive transitional periods and establishing stable civilian governance.

ly.headline: Libyan command vows response after two naval staff die in Benghazi attack
ly.dek: The General Command said the officers died from injuries sustained in an attack on Benghazi Port and explosions involving the targeted vessel.
paragraphs: Libya’s eastern-based General Command of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces said two members of its Naval Forces General Staff died after an attack on Benghazi Port. Chief Warrant Officer Tahir Abdullah Al-Sadiq and Lieutenant Ali Muhammad Al-Said succumbed to injuries sustained in the attack and subsequent explosions.

The command said the attack targeted a vessel at the port and pledged to seek justice for the two officers. It also said it would respond at a time and place of its choosing, without specifying a date or action.

Ukraine claimed responsibility for drone and unmanned sea vehicle attacks on Russian ships off the Benghazi coast and in the port early Monday, according to Libya Herald. The command said wounded people were recovering.

mg.headline: AFG Bank buys power producers’ Jirama claims for about 400 billion ariary
mg.dek: The 2026 deal gives independent electricity producers cash without waiting for the state utility to settle its debts.
paragraphs: AFG Bank Madagascar completed a purchase in 2026 of claims held by some independent electricity producers against Jirama, Madagascar’s national utility, for about 400 billion ariary. The transaction was presented at GEM Connect 2026, a business event held at the Novotel on 19 November.

The bank’s purchase gives the affected suppliers liquidity before Jirama pays their claims, helping them maintain operations and meet their own commitments, according to Midi Madagasikara. The state selected bank purchases of claims as one way to clear debts accumulated by the utility.

The operation followed 18 months of negotiations and structuring. The report also cites earlier bank financing in Madagascar, including a sustainable bond of about 38 million dollars issued by BRED Madagasikara at the end of 2024.

mg.dek: Six lawmakers are being discussed as possible successors, while negotiations and candidate filings continue ahead of Wednesday’s vote.
paragraphs: Madagascar’s deputies are due to elect a new president of the National Assembly on Wednesday, 25 November, after voting to remove Siteny Randrianasoloniaiko. In a late-night sitting at the Tsimbazaza Palace, 112 deputies backed his removal and 37 opposed it, Midi Madagasikara reported.

A total of 149 lawmakers took part in the vote, which also removed two vice-presidents and the assembly’s third questor. Marco Tsaradia, a deputy and vice-president for the former province of Toliara, is among six lawmakers discussed as a possible successor, Madagascar Tribune reported.

The other names include lawmakers Fanomezantsoa Andrianjanahary, Zavamanitra Andriamiharivolamena, Fidèle Razara Pierre, Fetra Ralambozafimbololona and minister Hanitra Razafimanantsoa. Candidacies were due to close on Wednesday morning; deputies must also fill the other vacant bureau posts.

mg.headline: Madagascar puts 118 protected areas under daily satellite watch
mg.dek: The system tracks fires and deforestation, with verified critical alerts in core zones sent to site managers within 24 hours.
paragraphs: Madagascar's Foundation for Protected Areas and Biodiversity has begun daily satellite monitoring of fires and deforestation across 118 terrestrial protected areas. The foundation presented its Control Room on 23 November at its headquarters in Ankadivato, with support from Conservation Allies and Madagascar National Parks.

The system combines satellite alerts, ranked by ecological severity, with information on human pressures such as clearing, illegal logging, charcoal production and gold mining. It also records conservation work, including patrols logged through the Spatial Monitoring and Reporting Tool. For a verified critical alert in a protected area's core zone, the Control Room will send managers maps and usable geographic coordinates within 24 hours, and managers remain responsible for action on their sites.

The data also feed an impact dashboard for 75 protected areas funded by the foundation. Its board chairman, Bruno Rajaspera, said the system should help target available funding and improve accountability for conservation spending.

mg.headline: Madagascar and Djibouti sign three accords and discuss port cooperation
mg.dek: The talks included proposals for training, digitised logistics and transport infrastructure, while Madagascar’s delegation visited Doraleh terminal.
paragraphs: Madagascar and Djibouti signed three cooperation accords on Tuesday, 24 November 2026, during the first day of Colonel Michaël Randrianirina’s official visit to Djibouti. The texts cover visa exemptions for diplomatic, official and service passport holders, a general cooperation framework and a memorandum on bilateral consultations.

Djibouti President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh proposed sharing his country’s port experience with Madagascar. He raised a joint committee, staff training, digitising logistics operations and developing transport and cargo-handling infrastructure. Madagascar’s delegation, which included Toamasina port’s director general, toured Doraleh’s container terminal.

The delegation saw the terminal’s cranes, storage areas and cargo-handling equipment. Madagascar wants to use Toamasina’s existing infrastructure and Djibouti’s expertise to improve terminal management and cargo movement. In 2025, Doraleh handled 1 062 067 20-foot equivalent units, while Toamasina recorded 267 701 over the same period.

mg.headline: Ericsson and YAS Madagascar launch technology training at Madagascar university
mg.dek: The programme, deployed at the University of Antsiranana from 18 November, targets students in computing, telecommunications and polytechnic studies.
paragraphs: Ericsson and YAS Madagascar, a subsidiary of the Yas group, have launched the Ericsson Educate 21st Century Technologies programme at the University of Antsiranana, in northern Madagascar. Deployed from 18 November, it targets university students, prioritising those studying computing, telecommunications and polytechnic subjects.

The programme provides access through computer laboratories equipped and supported by YAS on campus. Students can follow self-paced, interactive courses on mobile devices, using practical simulations to study 5G, artificial intelligence, the internet of things, automation, data science and cybersecurity.

Ericsson and YAS said the initiative is intended to prepare students for careers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics. It is linked to Madagascar's 2023-2028 Digital Strategic Plan, which prioritises strengthening human capabilities.

mw.headline: Malawi nurses warn shortages threaten deliveries and emergency surgery
mw.dek: The nurses’ organisation says missing medicines, anaesthetics and intravenous fluids put patients and health workers at risk across the country.
paragraphs: Malawi’s National Organisation of Nurses and Midwives says shortages of essential medical supplies are putting patients and frontline staff at risk. At Limbe Health Centre, expectant mothers were reportedly asked to contribute money for batteries for a blood pressure machine.

The organisation’s president, Shouts Simeza, said shortages of gloves and aprons leave nurses and midwives exposed to infections including HIV and hepatitis B. He said missing medicines, anaesthetics and intravenous fluids threaten deliveries and emergency Caesarean sections, while ambulance fuel shortages delay referrals.
The nurses’ body urged the government and health authorities to fix supply chain failures, increase funding and ensure hospitals and clinics receive critical supplies.

mw.headline: Malawi deregisters HRDC and 35 organisations, cutting off foreign funding
mw.dek: The US-based Human Rights Foundation says the decision threatens civic freedoms; seven civil society groups have challenged its legal basis.
paragraphs: Malawi’s NGO Regulatory Authority deregistered the Human Rights Defenders Coalition (HRDC) and 35 other organisations on Nov. 4, citing regulatory noncompliance. The decision bars the groups from receiving foreign funding, a major source of support for many civil society organisations.

The Human Rights Foundation, a New York-based advocacy organisation, criticised the move and said it threatens civic freedoms. HRDC, a platform of more than 200 organisations and individuals, had called for nationwide demonstrations demanding the resignation of Energy Minister Jean Mathanga over electricity blackouts and fuel shortages.
Seven civil society organisations challenged the deregistration days after it was announced, questioning whether authorities followed safeguards including the right to a fair hearing.

mw.headline: Malawi signs two IFAD deals worth $20m for farming projects
mw.dek: The funding will support climate resilience and tomato production, including a $452,000 grant through the China-IFAD SSTC Facility.
paragraphs: Malawi signed two financing agreements worth $20m, about K36 billion, with the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) in Lilongwe on Tuesday. The money will fund the Smallholder Climate Resilience Project and a programme to build tomato self-sufficiency through sustainable technologies and practices.

Finance minister Joseph Mathyola Mwanamvekha said climate change is harming smallholder farmers, with floods, droughts and tropical cyclones destroying crops, killing livestock and damaging infrastructure. IFAD country director for Malawi Bernadette Mukonyora said the partnership is intended to help farmers produce more, lose less and earn more.
The China-IFAD SSTC Facility will provide Malawi with a $452,000 grant, while the government will contribute $197,000.

mw.headline: Malawi construction regulator appoints acting chief as CEO moves to university
mw.dek: Board chair Peter Matipwiri says Gerald Khonje’s secondment to teach at Mubas took effect immediately under a letter dated November 23.
paragraphs: Gerald Khonje, chief executive of Malawi’s Construction Industry Regulatory Authority (Cira), has been seconded to teach at the Malawi University of Business and Applied Sciences (Mubas). The move took effect immediately, according to a November 23 letter to Cira staff from board chair Peter Matipwiri.

Cira has named Dorothy Nyong’a, its director of regulatory and compliance services, as acting chief executive until further notice. Khonje is among several chief executives deployed to Mubas; the others lead the Central Region Water Board, Blantyre Water Board, Southern Region Water Board and Electricity Supply Corporation of Malawi.

Benedicto Kondowe of the Civil Society Education Coalition said placing chief executives without academic backgrounds in universities undermines standards and distorts human-resource planning. Other senior officials have been sent to Mzuzu University and the University of Malawi, as well as public colleges.

ml.headline: Insecurity disrupts classes for 3 979 children in Mali
ml.dek: The UNICEF figure covers pupils affected by the crisis, while 639 students displaced from Kidal were counted in Gao after April 2026 violence.
paragraphs: Violence in Mali has disrupted classes for 3 979 children, according to UNICEF. In Gao, 639 pupils displaced from Kidal were counted after violence in April 2026, disrupting a school year already under way.

A special session allowed 24 displaced candidates to sit the Diplôme d’études fondamentales examinations. At the October 2026 school-year opening, 2 444 schools were reported non-functional, affecting more than 733 000 children; UNICEF said insecurity was the main cause.

Catch-up classes served 10 252 pupils across several regions in the third quarter, and six schools reopened in Gao with UNICEF and partner support. The organisation said some schools close again when threats persist.

ml.headline: Mali opens talks on fishing, livestock and aquaculture pressures
ml.dek: Representatives from six agroecological zones are contributing findings as herders report scarce pasture and fishers cite poor water quality and insecurity.
paragraphs: Mali opened national talks on fishing, livestock and aquaculture in Bamako on Monday, with the sessions scheduled to run through 25 November. The authorities say the discussions are intended to address problems including climate disruption and insecurity in the three sectors.

In Nioro du Sahel, herder Adama Diakité says grazing areas have become scarce and reduced rainfall has cut fodder supplies. In Mopti, fisher Yirimougou Diakité attributes declining fish numbers to river-water degradation linked to dredging; he says insecurity also keeps fishers from some distant areas. He called for training and suitable equipment.

Representatives from six agroecological zones have presented summaries of their work, said Drissa Coulibaly, an assistant to the organising commission. The findings are to be combined in a general report to guide sector development. Mali recorded production of 122 671 tonnes of fish and 157 775 tonnes of controlled meat in 2025; its 2026 fish target is 133 296 tonnes.

ml.dek: The tests also provided medicine or prescriptions to people who screened positive, while diabetes groups pressed for more affordable treatment.
paragraphs: Health workers held free diabetes awareness and screening at the Sogoniko displacement site in Mali during World Diabetes Day, seeking to identify people with the disease and connect them to care.

Dr Ba Traoré, an endocrinologist at Mali Hospital, said screening was open to everyone, not only displaced people. Several displaced people learned their blood-sugar status; those who tested positive received medicine or prescriptions when medicines were unavailable on site, displaced people’s spokesperson Amadou Tamboura said.

Karfa Maïga, head of Mali’s national federation of people with diabetes, welcomed government measures to lower prices for insulin and oral diabetes medicines, and called for continued support. The report says official estimates put the number living with diabetes in Mali between three hundred and fifty thousand and seven hundred thousand.

ml.headline: Baobab Mali offers women loans without opening or application fees
ml.dek: Its Crédit Muso loans range from CFA100.000 to CFA1.000.000 over 10 months, with interest still payable.
paragraphs: Baobab Mali offers women entrepreneurs Crédit Muso loans from CFA100.000 to CFA1.000.000 over 10 months, with no opening or application fees. The lender says the product is designed to help women finance their businesses.

Borrowers still pay interest and must repay on a schedule suited to their income. A shopkeeper may need money to increase stock, while a workshop owner may use a loan for raw materials and wages before a customer pays. Baobab says its advisers assess clients’ expenses, payment delays and quieter trading periods to determine what they can borrow and repay.

The product was discussed against recommendations from microfinance professionals who met in Bamako from 20 to 23 October 2026. The recommendations, reported on 2 November by the Treasury and Public Accounting Directorate, included a national guarantee mechanism covering women, young entrepreneurs and agriculture. Baobab has operated in Mali since 2013 and has 18 branches, nine outside Bamako.

ml.headline: Mali’s army says it freed 24 soldiers near Kidal
ml.dek: The army said its forces worked with Russian partners in an operation on 18 November in the In-Tebezas area, about 110 km from Kidal.
paragraphs: Mali’s army said it freed 24 soldiers held in the In-Tebezas area, about 110 km south-east of Kidal, on 18 November. The operation involved the Malian Armed Forces and Russian partners from Africa Corps, according to the army’s announcement.

At a reception on 23 November, army chief of staff Élysée Jean Dao said the soldiers had been captured during events in Kidal on 25 April. He credited intelligence, planning and coordination for locating the group holding them. The soldiers were received by Defence Minister Delegate Oumar Diarra.
Dao said the freed soldiers were ready to return to duty. One of them, Yaya Coulibaly, thanked the military authorities and President Assimi Goïta on behalf of his colleagues.

mr.headline: Mauritania launches Somelec power-network overhaul with French partners
mr.dek: EDF experts are due to assess Nouakchott’s distribution network in December, after August fires prompted authorities to seek a technical review.
paragraphs: Mauritania’s government has launched a development programme for state electricity company Somelec, drawing on expertise from France’s Électricité de France (EDF) and working with the French Development Agency. The first phase is a technical assessment of the electricity distribution network in Nouakchott.

EDF International Networks experts are expected to begin fieldwork in December, Energy and Petroleum Minister Mohamed Ould Abdel Fattah said at a ministry meeting on Monday, 23 November. The minister said the programme followed fires in August and would involve national teams and partners. Later phases will provide operational and network-management support with EDF International and RTE International, then develop a network-modernisation programme.

A technical committee will monitor implementation, prepare periodic progress reports and send them to the minister. The cooperation is also intended to improve network maintenance and strengthen Somelec’s technical skills.

mr.headline: Biram Dah Abeid resigns from Mauritania’s National Assembly
mr.dek: The opposition deputy announced his departure during a session on the government’s policy statement, after returning from Europe and the United States.
paragraphs: Biram Dah Abeid, a Mauritanian opposition deputy, resigned from the National Assembly during a session on the government’s policy statement. He said he had returned hurriedly from Europe and the United States after being summoned to attend and threatened with sanctions over repeated absences.

Prime Minister El Moctar Ould Djay was due to present the government’s general policy statement in plenary. Dah Abeid said he would use peaceful means to shake up national politics; the resignation prompted discussion in Nouakchott and elsewhere in the country.

In a later interview with Le Calame, Dah Abeid sought to explain his decision. The outlet’s commentary said the interview did not clarify his reasons, while reporting that people had since emerged seeking to link him to alleged financial and land-related wrongdoing.

mr.headline: Opposition party chief faults government over rising food prices
mr.dek: Mokhtar Ould Cheikh also condemned alleged privacy breaches and detainee-rights violations in a case involving 22 suspects sent to judicial investigation.
paragraphs: Mokhtar Ould Cheikh, head of Mauritania’s Union of Forces for Change party, accused the government of failing to contain rising prices for locally produced meat, dairy products and fish. He made the criticism at a party news conference in Nouakchott on Tuesday, saying the country was facing an unprecedented cost-of-living crisis.

Ould Cheikh said the government had not shifted from an economy reliant on raw-material exports to one that adds value to national resources, creates jobs and strengthens self-sufficiency. He also condemned what he called the disclosure of citizens’ personal data and violations of detainees’ rights in a case involving bloggers.

The public prosecutor sent 22 suspects for judicial investigation and sought pretrial detention for 15, on accusations including blackmail, money laundering and spreading false information. The prosecutor said the alleged acts threatened state security, national unity and civil peace.

paragraphs: Mauritania’s navy rescued a boat carrying 93 people off Nouadhibou on Monday as it travelled toward the Canary Islands, the army said in a statement published Tuesday.
The group comprised 69 men, 17 women and 7 minors. The army did not identify their nationalities or say where the boat had set off from.

mu.headline: Mauritius banks raise lending rates by 0.25%
mu.dek: MCB’s prime lending rate is 7.15% from 23 November, while Absa’s rose to 7.95% on 18 November.
paragraphs: Mauritius banks are raising lending rates by 0.25% from late November after the central bank’s Key Rate rose to 5% on 11 November. The change affects borrowers with housing and car loans, as well as people seeking new bank credit.

The Mauritius Commercial Bank (MCB) set its Prime Lending Rate at 7.15% from 23 November, and Absa’s rate reached 7.95% on 18 November. Ion News reported that the higher rates will increase loan instalments and total borrowing costs, reducing households’ monthly disposable income. Savings account rates are also rising.

The State Bank of Mauritius had not announced its new rate by publication. MauBank’s committee was scheduled to meet on 26 November, with new rates due that afternoon. The Mauritius Housing Company had applied the increase from 16 November.

mu.headline: Mauritius leaves femicide and marital-rape reforms unproclaimed
mu.dek: Parliament passed the Criminal Code changes in July, but they cannot take effect until they are formally proclaimed.
paragraphs: Mauritius has yet to proclaim Criminal Code amendments passed by Parliament in July 2026 that recognise femicide and remove the marital-rape exception. The provisions cannot take effect until proclamation, leaving their start date pending.

Mokshda Pertaub, a lawyer and president of the women’s rights organisation MPower, said the delay means the reforms remain unable to produce their intended legal effects. The amendments also set out aggravating circumstances for killings of women, including the relationship between the victim and alleged perpetrator, prior domestic abuse and the victim’s vulnerability.

A separate Domestic Abuse Act took effect on 14 September, extending protections to economic, emotional, psychological and digital abuse, as well as controlling behaviour and coercion. It covers current and former partners and replaced the 1997 domestic-violence law. MPower discussed implementation at a workshop in Péreybère on 22 November.
