mu.headline: Mauritius proposes committee on offences by children
mu.dek: The parliamentary inquiry would examine causes, parental responsibility, support services and whether to change the minimum age of criminal responsibility.
paragraphs: Mauritius’s Parliament is considering a committee to examine why children commit offences and engage in antisocial or violent behaviour. On Tuesday, 24 November, Speaker Shirin Aumeeruddy-Cziffra read out a motion from the prime minister proposing the committee.

The committee would assess whether to amend rules on parental responsibility and penalties for adults who encourage minors to offend. It would also review the capacity of institutions and staff working with children in conflict with the law, those with serious behavioural problems, children who are abandoned or out of school, and young people living on the streets.

The inquiry would also consider whether to change the minimum age of criminal responsibility. The Speaker said it could call people, request documents and consult specialists, including child psychologists, sociologists and anthropologists. The motion was put to a vote.

mu.headline: Port-Louis court grants bail to man charged in Iyempermal murder inquiry
mu.dek: Mohammad Reedwan Baulauck denies involvement and faces a provisional accusation of obstructing the course of justice.
paragraphs: A court in Port-Louis granted bail on Tuesday 24 November to Mohammad Reedwan Baulauck, who was arrested in the inquiry into Selven Iyempermal’s murder. Baulauck faces a provisional accusation of obstructing the course of justice and denies involvement.

The court set bail at Rs 75 000 and required Baulauck to sign a Rs 500 000 debt acknowledgment. He must report to the nearest police station to his home every Friday between 6 h and 18 h. The Major Crime Investigation Team arrested him on 5 November.

Iyempermal, 34, was attacked at a house in La Caverne, Vacoas, on the evening of 27 October and died at Candos hospital on 28 October. His friend told police that six armed, masked men had entered the house; an autopsy found he died from haemorrhagic shock caused by multiple injuries.

mz.headline: Mozambique's Supreme Court begins hearing 36 witnesses in Mondlane trial
mz.dek: The former presidential candidate faces five criminal charges, including incitement to terrorism, in a case heard at the court in Maputo.
paragraphs: Mozambique's Supreme Court began hearing witnesses on Wednesday in the trial of Venâncio Mondlane, a former presidential candidate charged with five crimes, including incitement to terrorism. The case is being heard in Maputo, and 36 witnesses are listed: 12 for the public prosecutor, four for the Mozambican road network company REVIMO, which joined the case as an assisting party, and 20 for Mondlane's defence.

The court is also due to hear three experts, including two from the mobile operators Tmcel and Vodacom. A technical expert from the Criminal Investigation Service (SERNIC), requested by prosecutors, is to assess the authenticity of an audio recording said to feature Mondlane and Albino Forquilha, leader of the opposition party PODEMOS (the Mozambican Democratic Party), discussing a plan to subvert the rule of law. Two declarants requested by the defence, activist Graça Machel and Brazilian businesswoman Samanta Lemos, are also listed; Lemos is to testify virtually.
Prosecutors' 12 witnesses were expected to testify over Wednesday and Thursday, followed by REVIMO's witnesses on Friday. Defence witnesses could begin on Monday, according to the report.

mz.headline: Mozambique approves 10 new higher-education institutions in a week
mz.dek: Five private institutions cleared on 24 November must still win approval of their teaching plans and licences before they can open.
paragraphs: Mozambique's Council of Ministers approved the creation of 10 higher-education institutions in decisions taken at its 33rd and 34th ordinary sessions, held on 17 and 24 November in Maputo. On 17 November, five were authorised, among them the Instituto Superior Baía de Moçambique in Pemba, the Instituto Superior Njerendje in Chimoio and the Universidade de Ciências e Tecnologias in Maputo.

A week later, the council approved five more by separate decrees, all private initiatives. They include the Universidade Sagrada Família, also known as Unisagrada, in Maxixe, Inhambane province, and the Universidade Trindade Cristã de Moçambique in Matola. Government spokesman Inocencio Impissa said the promoters will fund the institutions, with no construction or financing by the state planned.

Before approval, officials assessed the projects' initial infrastructure, planned teaching staff and organisation. Promoters must still obtain approval for teaching materials and complete licensing before activities begin. The government says the expansion aims to improve access, with gross enrolment at about 8.51%, below the Southern African Development Community average of 10.5%.

na.headline: Meatco proposes three-month wage cuts as exports remain suspended
na.dek: The state-owned processor says a 50% reduction in working hours from January would save about N$16.7 million, while December pay also faces cuts.
paragraphs: Namibia’s state-owned Meat Corporation of Namibia (Meatco) has proposed cutting ordinary working hours and basic pay by 50% for three months from 1 January, as suspended beef exports and weaker domestic demand squeeze revenue. The company announced the measures on Tuesday after consulting the Namibia Food and Allied Workers Union (NAFAU).

Employees without enough accrued annual leave would receive two-thirds of their usual December remuneration; those with sufficient leave would be paid in full using their leave. Meatco said November salaries would be paid in full. It estimates the proposed January-to-March cuts would save about N$16.7 million against a monthly wage bill above N$15.5 million.

Meatco plans to close its offices and production facilities from 4 December to 4 January. The company has also proposed deferring December’s 13th cheques until operations and cash flow normalise, while preserving employees’ entitlement subject to a formal union agreement. NAFAU secretary general Jacob Penda said the union would agree only to terms favourable to employees under their contracts.

na.headline: Namibia reports N$50.3m in payment fraud through October
na.dek: The Bank of Namibia says card, electronic funds transfer and electronic-money channels recorded the losses, with EFT fraud driving a first-half increase.
paragraphs: Namibia recorded N$50.3 million in reported fraud involving card, electronic funds transfer (EFT) and electronic-money payments from January to October 2026, Bank of Namibia Deputy Governor Leonie Dunn said at a Windhoek summit on Tuesday.

Financial institutions recovered about N$15.6 million in the first six months, equal to 48% of reported fraud value. EFT fraud rose 47.3% to N$21.9 million from N$14.8 million in the same period of 2025, while card fraud fell 10.8% to N$10.4 million and electronic-money fraud dropped 72.6% to about N$229,000. Dunn said victims often authorised EFT transfers after being manipulated, making recovery harder; no electronic-money fraud losses were recovered.

The central bank gazetted revised cybersecurity rules for banks and the national payment system in June and July. It is also working with the financial services industry to revise fraud rules, while a sector council is developing an incident response plan and information-sharing platform.

na.headline: Study projects N$313.74 billion annual GDP contribution from Namibia oil
na.dek: A Standard Bank Namibia-commissioned study ties the estimate to three offshore projects, while production has yet to begin and local benefits are not assured.
paragraphs: Namibia’s offshore oil industry could add an estimated N$313.74 billion a year to gross domestic product, according to an independent study commissioned by Standard Bank Namibia. The estimate covers the Venus, Capricornus and Mopane projects and is equivalent to US$18 billion at the indicative exchange rate of N$17.43 per US dollar published on 24 November.

The study was launched in Windhoek on Tuesday. Namibia has not started commercial oil production, and the eventual contribution depends on investment decisions, project approvals, development timelines and production levels. Local businesses could seek work in engineering, logistics, construction, transport, catering, marine services and technical support, but would need skills and supplier capacity to meet industry standards.

Cabinet approved the National Upstream Petroleum Local Content Policy on 4 August 2026. Kornelia Shilunga, the president’s special adviser and head of the Upstream Petroleum Unit, said local contracts, skilled jobs and transfers of technology and expertise would determine the policy’s success. The full study and its modelling assumptions had not been made public.

na.headline: Namibia wrestlers seek N$334 600 for Commonwealth championships
na.dek: The federation needs the funds by 27 November for accommodation, meals and a training camp in Polokwane, South Africa.
paragraphs: Namibia’s elite wrestlers are seeking financial support to compete at the Commonwealth Wrestling Championships in Polokwane, South Africa, from 3 to 7 December. The Namibia Wrestling Federation needs N$334 600 to cover accommodation, meals and a three-day international training camp for a 16-member delegation.

The team comprises 12 wrestlers, two coaches, a team leader and one official, competing in under-17, under-20 and senior categories. The federation said the money is needed by 27 November to meet payment deadlines set by the host federation. About 80% of the squad comes from the Ministry of Gender Equality and Child Welfare’s Afterschool Centre wrestling club.

The federation is offering sponsorship packages from N$1 500, which covers one wrestler’s tournament meals, up to the full delegation cost. The championships are part of the team’s preparation for the 2027 African Continental Championships and African Games.

ne.headline: Niger reports 81 flood deaths and 131 injured by 31 October
ne.dek: Floods also affected 97 334 people and destroyed 12 985 homes, according to the population ministry’s representative.
paragraphs: Niger recorded 81 deaths and 131 people injured in floods by 31 October 2026, Sani Douda, representing the minister of Population, Social Action and National Solidarity, said on 24 November in Maradi. The floods affected 97 334 people across 13 976 households.

The toll also includes 12 985 houses that collapsed and 1 366 head of livestock killed, Douda said. Officials and partners met in Maradi to review the 2026 response, identify shortcomings and recommend ways to improve flood prevention and management in 2027.

Douda said the year’s work included strengthening early-warning systems, operational preparedness and community mobilisation. Gaspard Cirhalwirwa, the World Food Programme’s deputy head of office in Maradi, said the agency would continue supporting Niger’s disaster-prevention and management efforts.

ne.headline: Niger opens investor forum with 30 project proposals
ne.dek: Prime Minister Ali Mahamane Lamine Zeine said the projects cover agriculture, mining, energy, infrastructure and other sectors.
paragraphs: Niger opened its first International Forum to Invest in Niger in Niamey on Tuesday, 24 November 2026, with Prime Minister Ali Mahamane Lamine Zeine presenting about 30 investment dossiers to national and international investors. The proposals cover agriculture and agro-industry, mines, oil and gas, energy, transport and communications infrastructure, and groundwater.

Zeine said the country had revised its investment code in February 2025. He said it provides equal treatment regardless of investors’ nationality, protects private property and allows the transfer of income, profits and sale proceeds. The code also says later legislation cannot reduce benefits granted under an investment approval.

Zeine identified insecurity as the main constraint on investment and said a national force had been established specifically to protect major investments and supply corridors. He said the force offers tailored security plans to investors.

ne.headline: Yogo’s Toubou chiefdom traces more than 125 years of local rule
ne.dek: The Niger community near Chad’s border has had five chiefs since its official creation in 1900, with a new leader elected in 2025.
paragraphs: Yogo, a Toubou chiefdom in Niger’s N’Gourti department, has been led by five successive chiefs since its official creation in 1900, according to Agence Nigerienne de Presse. The settlement lies four kilometres from the Chad border and is home to the Yiriya Kedelaya community.

Current chief Kedella Hamet Kedella Botrane was elected on 5 March 2025 to succeed his elder brother. The chiefdom’s leaders have included Kedella Kalli Okimi, who held the post from 1914 to 1968, and Kedella Ali Kedella Botrane, who led from 2002 until his death in 2024.

The community’s history goes back to a larger chiefdom founded around 1800, according to genealogies relayed by the current chief. Residents have traditionally raised camels and goats and traded across the border, while maintaining family and economic ties on both sides.

ne.headline: Agadez governor thanks religious scholars for prayers for peace in Niger
ne.dek: Governor Ibra Boulama Issa attended a Quran reading and prayers at Amiskini Mosque, where he relayed thanks from President Abdourahamane Tiani.
paragraphs: Agadez Governor Ibra Boulama Issa attended a Quran reading followed by prayers for peace and prosperity at Amiskini Mosque on Tuesday, 24 November. The Secretary General of the Agadez region, the delegated administrator of Agadez urban commune, the Sultan of Aïr, religious leaders, security force officials and civil-society representatives also attended.

Boulama said the prayers asked God to bless Niger, its people and its leaders, and to keep the country a land of peace, serenity and prosperity. He also asked that the country's security forces, who he said fight daily to defend its territory, be blessed and supported, and that the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) remain an area of peace and development.

Boulama thanked and congratulated the religious scholars on behalf of President Abdourahamane Tiani, and passed on thanks from the prime minister and the whole government. He urged them to keep multiplying such prayers for Niger.

rw.headline: Rwandans report widespread digital fraud, with money and gift card scams most common
rw.dek: A TransUnion survey finds 62% of Rwandans surveyed were targeted by digital fraud, and most fear their identities will be used to commit crimes.
paragraphs: A TransUnion survey found that 62% of Rwandans surveyed were targeted by email, online, phone-call or text-message fraud during a recent three-month period. Money or gift card scams were the most reported scheme, cited by 43% of those targeted.

In TransUnion’s Q1 2026 Consumer Pulse Study, 62% of respondents said their greatest worry beyond access to credit cards or financial accounts was someone using their identity to commit a crime. Another 45% feared criminals would gain access to workplace systems. Phone-call scams designed to extract personal information were reported by 30% of those targeted.

Fake social media profiles concerned 52% of respondents, email phishing 51% and viruses or malware 46%. Didier Mutabazi, chief executive of TransUnion Rwanda, said criminals are combining stolen identities, compromised credentials and AI-powered deception to target consumers at scale.

rw.headline: Rwanda elects new mayors in 18 of 27 districts
rw.dek: Nine outgoing mayors were returned to office in the November 24 elections, which saw women take eight of the district leadership posts.
paragraphs: 18 of Rwanda's 27 districts elected new mayors after the November 24 elections, while nine outgoing leaders secured another five-year term.

The new leadership comprises 19 men and eight women, so women hold 29.63% of the mayoral posts and men 70.37%. The eight districts under women leadership are Musanze, Ngoma, Nyabihu, Gakenke, Kamonyi, Rwamagana, Rulindo and Ruhango. Six of the eight women are taking up the posts for the first time, while Vestine Mukandayisenga of Gakenke and Nathalie Niyonagira of Ngoma have retained theirs.

Returning mayors include Gerald Muzungu of Karongi, Narcisse Mupenzi of Nyamasheke, Phanuel Sindayiheba of Rusizi, Fred Hategekimana of Kayonza, Prosper Mulindwa of Rubavu, Bruno Rangira of Kirehe and Henry Kakooza of Nyagatare. Their election to the new district councils let them seek another term on the district executive committees.

rw.headline: Rwanda weighs avocado export plans at three-day industry meeting
rw.dek: Growers, exporters and officials are reviewing production, quality and market access as Rwanda seeks more foreign exchange from avocados.
paragraphs: Rwandan avocado growers, exporters and officials have begun a three-day meeting to discuss ways to increase production, improve quality and reach more international markets. The discussions cover the chain from cultivation and harvesting through processing, packaging and distribution.

Sandrine Urujeni, deputy chief executive for operations at the National Agricultural Export Development Board (NAEB), said the board would work with government agencies, development partners and private businesses to develop commercial avocado farming. Participants are also reviewing findings from an avocado farming census intended to show industry performance, gaps and investment needs.

The census is expected to inform measures to raise productivity, increase value addition and diversify export destinations. The report says Rwanda’s landlocked position makes transport costs and logistics important to export competitiveness.

rw.dek: Division commanders from Uganda and Rwanda have opened the 9th UPDF/RDF Proximity Commanders' Meeting, aimed at military cooperation and cross-border security.
paragraphs: Officers of the Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) arrived in Rwanda on Tuesday for the three-day 9th UPDF/RDF Proximity Commanders' Meeting. The meeting is aimed at strengthening military cooperation and cross-border security.

The Ugandan delegation is led by Major General Paul Muhanguzi, commander of the UPDF's 2 Division. The Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) delegation is led by Maj Gen Ruki Karusisi, commander of the RDF's 2 Division.
Eastern Province Governor Prudence Rubingisa accompanied both delegations and joined residents of Tabagwe Village in a civil-military cooperation (CIMIC) tree-planting exercise.

rw.headline: Rwandan scholar wins South Africa’s Best Doctoral Student Award
rw.dek: Dr. Claudine Nkeragutabara Ndimurukundo received the honour at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research’s 2026 awards.
paragraphs: Dr. Claudine Nkeragutabara Ndimurukundo, a Rwandan scholar with a PhD in Human Genetics, won the Best Doctoral Student Award at South Africa’s 2026 Council for Scientific and Industrial Research Excellence Awards on 20 November.

Nkeragutabara said the award recognised her contributions to microbiome research. Rwanda’s High Commission in South Africa said her recognition celebrated Rwandan talent contributing to scientific research in South Africa and pointed to opportunities for collaboration between the two countries.

The annual awards recognise contributions to research, innovation and technology addressing societal challenges. South Africa’s Deputy Minister of Science, Technology and Innovation, Dr. Nomalungelo Gina, addressed scientific sovereignty and AI governance at the ceremony.

st.headline: São Tomé government completes cabinet with two appointments
st.dek: Economy Minister Orlando da Mata and Youth, Sport and Media Secretary of State Adnilson Rosa were sworn in at the presidential palace.
paragraphs: São Tomé and Príncipe’s 20th constitutional government completed its formation on 24 Nov. with the swearing-in of Economy, Energy and Digital Transformation Minister Orlando Borges da Mata and Youth, Sport and Media Secretary of State Adnilson de Sousa Pereira Rosa. President Carlos Vila Nova presided over the ceremony at the presidential palace.

Prime Minister Américo Ramos said his government was working on a programme to submit to the National Assembly. He said it must fit the country’s financial resources and the funding it can mobilise from partners.

Ramos named energy, health, education and infrastructure among the government’s priorities, alongside social sectors affecting the population. The two officials join the other members sworn in on Thursday, STP Press reported.

st.headline: Sao Tome police detain four over suspected illegal sand extraction
st.dek: The law requires a licence or authorisation for extraction and permits fines of 25.000,00 to 75.000,00 dobras for a serious offence.
paragraphs: Sao Tome and Principe’s National Police detained four people on suspicion of illegally extracting sand, Tela Non reported. The country’s Law No. 9/2020 requires a licence for extraction above 500 m³ and authorisation for smaller quantities.

Tela Non said that extracting sand without the required permission may be treated as a serious offence, carrying a fine of 25.000,00 to 75.000,00 dobras. The law also permits up to 20 m³ to be removed from private property, but only with a prior request and approval from the competent authority.

The detainees have not been convicted, and they are entitled to defend themselves, the report said. The law also provides for compensation for environmental damage; serious damage may bring criminal liability.

st.headline: São Tomé plans solar mini-grids for three isolated communities
st.dek: The project will upgrade Santa Adelaide’s existing solar system and prepare tariff rules for the new networks.
paragraphs: São Tomé and Príncipe plans solar-powered mini-grids for Ilhéu das Rolas, Santa Adelaide and Plateau, three hard-to-reach communities on São Tomé island. The initiative is supported by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) through its Africa Minigrids programme.

Belizardo Neto, director-general of natural resources and energy, said the systems will pair solar panels with batteries. Santa Adelaide already has solar power and storage, and upgrades are planned to improve its efficiency and capacity. The project is intended to support productive and economic activities as well as household use.

Public- and private-sector representatives are receiving training on tariffs for the future networks, with support from the African Forum of Utility Regulators. UNDP portfolio manager Maite Mendizabal said users must contribute to operating and maintenance costs, including battery replacement and repairs.

sn.headline: Court restores Senegal as Afcon 2025 champions
sn.dek: The arbitration panel overturned the decision that stripped Senegal of the title after its players left the field during the final against Morocco.
paragraphs: Senegal have been restored as Africa Cup of Nations 2025 winners after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned a decision stripping them of the title. The ruling leaves standing Senegal’s 1-0 extra-time victory over host Morocco in January.

The court’s three-member panel ruled unanimously after hearing an appeal by Senegal’s football federation in Lausanne on 8 October. Senegal had walked off in second-half stoppage time to protest a penalty; after returning, they completed the match and Pape Gueye scored the winner.
Morocco’s football federation said it would pursue “all necessary legal avenues”. The Confederation of African Football said it respected the arbitration ruling and would implement it.

sn.headline: Sports tribunal restores Senegal’s 1-0 Africa Cup final win
sn.dek: The court overturned a March ruling that had awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory by forfeit after Senegalese players briefly left the field.
paragraphs: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Tuesday restored Senegal’s 1-0 victory over Morocco in the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations final in Rabat, overturning a ruling that had awarded Morocco a 3-0 win by forfeit. The decision, dated 24 November, upheld Senegal’s appeal.

The three-arbitrator panel said the referee alone had authority to decide whether play should resume or end. Senegalese players had temporarily left the field in protest after Morocco was awarded a penalty; when play restarted, Senegal’s goalkeeper saved Brahim Díaz’s kick, and Senegal scored the final’s only goal in extra time. CAS said the players’ departure was serious but found no error of law in the referee’s decision to resume the match.

The ruling annulled the African football confederation’s appeals jury decision of 17 March and restored its disciplinary panel’s 11 February rejection of Morocco’s complaint. Morocco’s football federation will pay two-thirds of the arbitration costs, with the confederation covering the remaining third.

sn.headline: Senegal seminar examines management of borders with Gambia and Guinea-Bissau
sn.dek: Researchers and specialists met in Ziguinchor to discuss how land and maritime boundaries can support peace and cooperation among the three countries.
paragraphs: Researchers and specialists from Senegal, Gambia and Guinea-Bissau met on Tuesday, 24 November, at Assane Seck University in Ziguinchor for an international seminar on managing their land and maritime borders. The event was organised by the university’s legal and political sciences unit with the University of Caen Normandy in France.

Unit director Geneviève Bremond said disputed boundaries and land allocation can create tensions for communities living in affected areas. She said changes to borders could bring socio-economic difficulties and urged that residents be included in decisions to help prevent conflict among the three countries. Deputy director Khalifa Ababacar Kane said discussion of boundary definitions and the texts governing them could help resolve some disputes.
The first day also included presentations on border defence. Organisers hope the seminar’s conclusions will help residents understand territorial limits and live and work together peacefully.

sn.dek: Senegal has two contenders, while Morocco leads with three; the winner will be announced at the CAF Awards in Lagos on 2 December.
paragraphs: The Confederation of African Football (CAF) named Senegal’s Sadio Mané and Pape Gueye among five finalists for its 2026 African Player of the Year award on Wednesday, 25 November. Morocco has three contenders: Achraf Hakimi, Brahim Diaz and Ismaïl Saibari.

Mané, who won the award in 2019 and 2022, is seeking a third title. Gueye scored the extra-time winner against Morocco in the Africa Cup of Nations final in Rabat and was named in the tournament’s team of the tournament.

Senegal forward Ismaïla Sarr was left off the list despite winning the Africa Cup of Nations and the Conference League with Crystal Palace. The winner will be announced at the CAF Awards in Lagos, Nigeria, on Wednesday, 2 December, from 19:00 local time.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone charcoal trade sustains burners as tree loss threatens food security
sl.dek: A 65-year-old burner says his family depends on the work, while the environmental agency warns that economic trees are being cut.
paragraphs: Pa Alimamy, a 65-year-old charcoal burner in Sierra Leone, says the trade has kept him alive for more than two decades and supports his entire family. Charcoal is widely used in Freetown and other regional headquarters, where demand is rising against alternative cooking methods.

Paul Lamin, the Environmental Protection Agency’s director of natural resource governance, told Politico SL that burners are cutting economic trees such as orange and mango, leaving land bare and threatening food security. He said trees take a long time to grow back, and acknowledged that people have limited alternative energy options. The government’s National Energy Compact says only 36% of the population has access to electricity and clean cooking access is 15%.

The Food and Agriculture Organization estimates traditional wood energy emits 1/2.4 GT of carbon dioxide equivalent each year, or 2-7% of total human-caused greenhouse gas emissions; sub-Saharan Africa accounts for one third of emissions from wood energy.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone regulator reports NLE 7.4 million in 2024 revenue
sl.dek: The electricity and water watchdog collected the money from levies and licenses, up from NLE 2.3 million in 2023.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone's Electricity and Water Regulatory Commission (SLEWRC), the state body that licenses and oversees electricity and water providers, recorded NLE 7.4 million in internal revenue from levies and licenses in 2024, compared with NLE 2.3 million in 2023. The New Leone (NLE) is the country's currency.

Deputy Director Sama Sandi told the Ministry of Finance's budget discussions that the commission received no ministry funding for its recurrent spending in the 2023 and 2024 financial years, even though it had budgeted for it. In 2023, it took enforcement action against 64 non-compliant water companies, and its reports showed 80% of complaints were resolved within a week.

Sandi said the commission had developed a solar mini-grid tariff model that was close to completion. He submitted a budget of NLE 5,590.29 for the 2025 to 2027 financial years, and the commission's stated plans include monitoring tariff rates and expanding access.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone signs US$21.9 million phone assembly deal
sl.dek: The agreement with Gambian company Unique Group proposes a phased facility, with training, device testing and repairs included.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone signed a US$21.9 million memorandum of understanding with Gambian company Unique Group on November 19 to explore building a mobile phone and electronics assembly facility in the country. Al Musaed said 50 labour visas had been issued to Sierra Leoneans in the previous month. The proposed training facility would assess and screen applicants and equip them with skills before travel. sl.headline: Sierra Leone analysis questions vice president’s path to presidency
sl.dek: A political economist argues the office has often lacked a clear succession route, citing Solomon Ekuma Berewa’s 2007 election defeat.
paragraphs: A February 2026 analysis by Foday M. Daboh, a public policy analyst and political economist, argues that Sierra Leone’s vice presidency has not provided a reliable route to the presidency. The 1991 Constitution gives the office a role in continuity, but governments have often used it to balance regional, religious or ethnic interests and party factions, Daboh writes.

Daboh points to Solomon Ekuma Berewa, vice president during the Kabbah era, who ran as the Sierra Leone People’s Party candidate in 2007 and lost to Ernest Bai Koroma. He says Berewa’s defeat showed that governing experience and continuity did not guarantee election, and notes that no vice president has ever been elected president.
The analysis also cites former vice presidents Sorie Ibrahim Koroma, Francis Minah, Victor Bockarie Foh and Samuel Sam-Sumana, whose political paths did not produce a presidential succession.

so.headline: Somalia's prime minister replaces defence minister with Saadaq Joon
so.dek: The appointment comes as the country prepares for a security handover and the African Union mission's mandate expires on 31 December.
paragraphs: Somali Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre removed Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi on Monday and immediately appointed lawmaker Saadaq Omar Mohamed Hassan, known as Saadaq Joon, in his place. The decree cited Article 120 of Somalia's Provisional Constitution and consultations with the president, but gave no formal reason beyond Fiqi leaving the post.

Fiqi, who had held the defence role since April 2025, later accused unnamed politicians of urging soldiers to desert their positions. He also claimed that recent operations had killed more than 285 Al-Shabaab fighters and 12 commanders. Fiqi welcomed Joon in a separate statement and pledged support.

Joon is a former Banadir Regional Police commander and a current member of parliament. Somalia is recruiting additional soldiers as foreign forces hand over bases and the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission's United Nations mandate approaches its 31 December expiry.

so.headline: Somalia’s speaker accuses Kenya, Ethiopia and Uganda of colluding with Al-Shabaab
so.dek: Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur alleges Israel has assembled the countries, the militants and forces loyal to a former regional leader against Mogadishu.
paragraphs: Somalia’s parliamentary speaker, Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur, accused Kenya, Ethiopia and Uganda of colluding with Al-Shabaab in an address in Mogadishu. He alleged that Israel had assembled the three countries, the militants and forces loyal to former South West State leader Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen into a front against Somalia’s federal government.

Nur also said unnamed foreign powers sought to colonise Somalia and described the security structure backing the government as compromised. His remarks come as Laftagareen’s forces hold towns in the Bay region, where Ethiopian troops serving with the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia remain deployed. Mogadishu has accused Laftagareen’s camp of links to Al-Shabaab; his supporters deny the allegations.

Nur, elected speaker in August, made similar accusations against Kenya in October and urged the government to seek explanations from Nairobi. Kenyan officials said then that they had received no formal diplomatic complaint.

ss.headline: South Sudan rules out forced evictions as it maps six national parks
ss.dek: The government will consult residents, verify land claims and negotiate any relocation under proposed guidance for protected areas.
paragraphs: South Sudan will negotiate with communities living inside its six national parks before considering relocation, the Ministry of Wildlife Conservation and Tourism said. The government is developing guidance to set park boundaries and address settlement expansion into protected areas.

Martin Ring Malek, the ministry’s assistant director general for administration and finance, said authorities would first map boundaries and check whether residents had historical land claims. People who say they inherited land before a park was established must provide evidence, he said. The government has not established how many people live in the parks.

The verification will involve the ministries responsible for wildlife, land and environment, as well as the Land Commission, which will provide ownership documents and maps. Officials may adjust boundaries where evidence supports communities’ claims.

ss.headline: Western Equatoria trains 619 police recruits for 2027 elections
ss.dek: The recruits, including 37 women, are training at three sites as police prepare to secure polling stations instead of the army.
paragraphs: Western Equatoria State is training 619 police recruits in Yambio, Maridi and Mvolo ahead of South Sudan's planned February 2027 elections. The group includes 37 women, and 57 trainers are overseeing the programme, Musa Daud Kodi, its chairperson, said.

Registration and mobilisation ran from August 10 to August 20, 2026, and training had been underway for just over two months, Kodi said. Caretaker Governor Daniel Badagbu Rimbasa said police would secure polling stations and be deployed across the state to maintain public order and protect communities.

During a Tuesday visit to recruits at the State Police Headquarters in Yambio, Badagbu handed over uniforms and boots. He said the state would refer issues requiring national intervention to authorities in Juba and arrange medical personnel when needed; medical supplies had already arrived from Juba.

ss.headline: Juba council arrests 14 over soak pit violations in Hai Sujun
ss.dek: Enforcement teams are stepping up action against homes and businesses that discharge wastewater onto public streets.
paragraphs: Juba City Council arrested about 14 people in Hai Sujun, a neighbourhood in South Sudan's capital, on Tuesday for violating public health regulations that require households and businesses to install soak pits and septic tanks. The arrests followed the council's November 11 compliance deadline.

Enforcement teams later moved to Munuki, where they told restaurant operators that businesses must also comply with the regulations. The council said properties without proper systems were discharging wastewater onto public streets.

The action follows a weekly cleaning campaign in Hai Cinema led by Deputy Mayor for Environment and Waste Management Stephen Lomude, who raised concerns over properties lacking proper disposal systems. The council says it is stepping up enforcement.

ss.headline: South Sudan pitches investors on farming, livestock and fisheries
ss.dek: At a trade forum in Ethiopia, Trade Minister Labanya Margret Mathya cited land, livestock and a fisheries sector she said could earn US$300 million annually.
paragraphs: South Sudan’s caretaker trade minister, Dr. Labanya Margret Mathya, urged African and international investors to explore the country’s farming, livestock and fisheries sectors at the Africa Development Trade Forum 2026 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on Monday. She said South Sudan has approximately 30 million hectares of potentially arable land, with about 2.57 million hectares currently used for agriculture.

Mathya said the country has more than 18.8 million cattle and approximately 38.4 million domestic animals in total, and urged investors to consider meat processing, leather and other livestock businesses. She also cited World Bank figures putting fisheries’ annual potential at approximately US$300 million and called for partnerships with fishing and fish-processing companies.
The minister cited annual revenue potential of approximately US$550 million from shea butter, alongside investment prospects in gum Arabic, petroleum, gold and cobalt.

ss.headline: Juba academic proposes China-South Sudan governance research centre
ss.dek: Dr. Jackline Benjamin Libo Warille says it would link universities to produce policy advice and train public servants.
paragraphs: Dr. Jackline Benjamin Libo Warille, a lecturer at the University of Juba's School of Social and Economic Studies, proposed a China-South Sudan governance research centre at a roundtable in Juba on Tuesday. Universities in both countries would work together on research and advice to government institutions.

Covering public administration, public financial management, economic development, trade, industrialisation, gender inclusion and human development, the centre would be judged by its usefulness, Warille said. Training for public servants, independent policy dialogue and monitoring of government reforms would also be part of its work.

Warille said the 35% affirmative-action provision for women was not being adequately implemented and called for greater participation in political parties and public institutions. Chinese Ambassador Ma Qiang said China was ready to deepen governance and development exchanges as South Sudan prepares for its first general elections since independence.

sd.headline: Women's rights group reports 28 abductions and 15 sexual-violence cases in Blue Nile
sd.dek: The women and girls were fleeing fighting, while more than 7,000 families are making their way towards Damazin, local responders estimate.
paragraphs: The Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa (SIHA Network), a women's rights organisation working across the region, reported that 28 women and girls were abducted while fleeing fighting in Damazin, Sudan’s Blue Nile state. It also recorded 15 cases of conflict-related sexual violence against girls under 18.

The organisation said fighters from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias abducted the women and girls as they tried to reach safer areas. A first-response group told SIHA that one woman, a recent university graduate, contacted her family from a compound in Balgawa, an area under RSF control. SIHA said the 15 reported cases involved armed men in RSF uniforms near the villages of Elias and Armadolu.

Local responders cited by SIHA estimate more than 7,000 families are heading towards Damazin; many displaced people have travelled for days without safe drinking water. SIHA said renewed fighting had displaced thousands across the state.

sd.headline: Eight aid agencies assess needs after poor season in South Darfur
sd.dek: The delegation met residents in Manawashi and is checking water, healthcare and education services before deciding what humanitarian support is needed.
paragraphs: A delegation from eight United Nations agencies and international humanitarian organisations is assessing living conditions and community needs in Mershing locality, South Darfur, after what local authorities described as one of the area’s worst agricultural seasons. Farmers and pastoralists are among those most affected by the deteriorating situation.

Mershing executive director Oqba Abdelhamid told Radio Dabanga that delegates met residents in Manawashi to hear complaints and identify needs. The group includes the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, the World Health Organization and the World Food Programme, alongside five international organisations.

The programme also covers field visits to assess water, healthcare and education services. Abdelhamid said the delegation was due to visit Mershing town on Tuesday before continuing to El Malam locality; the assessment is intended to guide humanitarian interventions.

sd.headline: Sudan mine pond poisons 62 sheep and goats in Talodi
sd.dek: The Human Rights and Development Organisation says the livestock died after drinking from a gold-processing pond at the Mridan mine in South Kordofan.
paragraphs: 62 sheep and goats died after drinking from a gold-processing pond at the Mridan gold mine in Talodi, South Kordofan, on 7 November, according to the Human Rights and Development Organisation, known as the HUDO Centre. The animals belonged to Ismail Hussein Hamed, who filed a complaint with Talodi police and the Sudanese Mineral Resources Company.

The HUDO Centre said both authorities had been notified but had taken no decisive action. According to the mine committee, the company suspended the pond operator in September 2026 and fined him SDG 150 million, equivalent to USD 15,000, for breaching mining regulations. The operator then handed the site to the company, which left the pond open without treating its water.

The HUDO Centre has called on the company to rehabilitate the mine site and remove the contaminated ponds. Activists in the Talodi area have warned that toxic substances could reach reservoirs that supply the town.

tg.dek: The proposed institution would manage public and private deposits and invest them in projects including housing, health, education, water and renewable energy.

tg.headline: Paris court sets 7 December trial for Bolloré over Togo campaign
tg.dek: The French businessman faces foreign public official bribery and complicity charges tied to campaign communications and a Lomé port concession.
paragraphs: Vincent Bolloré is due before a Paris criminal court from 7 December 2026 on charges of bribing a foreign public official and complicity in breach of trust, in a case linked to Togo’s 2010 presidential campaign. The judicial investigation opened 13 years ago, according to Icilome.

Prosecutors allege that Bolloré and two other defendants arranged communication services for the Togolese president’s re-election campaign at an undervalued price of 100 000 euros. They also allege that the group’s payment for campaign work was connected to the extension of its Lomé port concession, held since 2001.

The case also concerns alleged tax advantages and construction of a third quay. Investigators opened a preliminary inquiry in July 2012 after a financial intelligence alert; a judicial investigation followed in November 2013.

tg.headline: Togo closes mosque and extends church suspension over noise complaints
tg.dek: The government says the measures enforce limits of 70 decibels by day and 55 at night under a 2025 order.
paragraphs: Togo’s territorial administration minister, Hodabalo Awaté, ordered the closure of Housseni mosque in Ségbé Adélankomé and extended the suspension of Fire Mountain Kingdom Ebenezer church in Nukafu by one month. The decisions followed complaints about noise at the places of worship.

The measures apply an interministerial order dated 20 February 2025, which sets permitted sound levels at 70 decibels during the day and 55 at night. The government said it intends to enforce the rules and protect residents’ peace.
Authorities also announced stronger inspections and awareness efforts with religious leaders and other affected parties. The report did not give a date for those actions.

tg.headline: Togo assigns road company maintenance target of 1 700 km for 2027
tg.dek: The target is in the 2027-2029 programme budget, while the government has not specified the cost of the work.
paragraphs: Togo’s government has set a 2027 target for maintaining 1 700 km of roads, according to the state’s 2027-2029 programme budget, as reported by Togo First. The work falls to the new National Road Financing Company, SONAFIR, which replaced the former road-maintenance financing company.

SONAFIR has been operating for a few weeks and has been led by Naka Gnassingbé de Souza since October 2026. The cost of maintaining the targeted roads has not been stated. The 2027 finance bill has not yet been finally adopted.

The government also plans studies on nearly 2 000 km of other routes. Road maintenance had previously relied mainly on fuel excise duties and toll revenue, which accounted for 70% and 30% of the former company’s resources, respectively.

tg.headline: Togo begins 16-day campaign against violence toward women and girls
tg.dek: The guidance covers physical, psychological, sexual, economic and online abuse, and sets out ways victims and witnesses can seek help.
paragraphs: Togo’s 16-day campaign against violence toward women and girls began on 25 November and is due to run through 10 December, the international Human Rights Day. The campaign offers guidance on recognising abuse and seeking help.

The advice identifies physical abuse, threats and humiliation, forced sexual acts, economic control and online harassment or threats as forms of violence. Victims and witnesses are urged to seek a safe place, tell someone they trust, obtain medical care and preserve evidence such as messages or witness names. They can report abuse to police or gendarmerie, or seek support from a victims’ association.
For people supporting a victim, the guidance recommends listening without judgment, respecting her pace and offering to accompany her to health care or a support service.

tn.headline: Tunisie Telecom pays 46.1% of state firms’ 2025 distributions
tn.dek: The telecom operator contributed 49.7 million dinars of 107.9 million, while total distributions fell 73% from 2024.
paragraphs: Tunisie Telecom paid 49.7 million dinars in dividends for 2025, accounting for 46.1% of the 107.9 million dinars in dividends and surpluses recorded for the Tunisian state from public companies. The figures cover the 2025 financial year.

An analysis by TeraFinances, published on 23 November and based on a report attached to the 2027 draft finance law, ranks the National Agricultural Bank second with 25.9 million dinars and the Tunisian Banking Company third with 22.2 million. Together, the three firms supplied 90.7% of the total. State distributions were 107.9 million dinars in 2025, down from 398.9 million in 2024 and 605.3 million in 2023.

The report’s 2025 figures exclude dividends from the Tunisian Petroleum Activities Company and the National Petroleum Distribution Company, both major contributors in 2024. The total remains provisional.

tn.headline: Zenith suspends $573 million arbitration against Tunisia
tn.dek: The energy group says its British subsidiaries will stop advancing Tunisia’s unpaid share of the arbitration costs, delaying a final ruling.
paragraphs: Zenith Energy has suspended its international arbitration against Tunisia after its three British subsidiaries stopped advancing the country’s unpaid share of the proceedings’ costs, the company said on Tuesday. The claims concern oil concessions at Sidi El Kilani and Ezzaouia and total nearly $573 million, excluding interest.

The case was registered with the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes in June 2023. Zenith says the final ruling, initially expected in May 2027, could be delayed by several months because the written submissions after hearings are complete but costs remain unpaid. The company said a procedural order dated 14 July 2025 allows the tribunal to consider unpaid advances when it makes its final allocation of costs.

Zenith said it is open to a negotiated settlement with Tunisian authorities, assisted by CNQ Global Advisors. The suspension does not end the case or withdraw the compensation claims, and the announcement has yet to be confirmed by the arbitration centre or Tunisian authorities.

tn.headline: Tunisie Freelance holds client payments until work is approved
tn.dek: The Tunisian platform says it has more than 34 000 members and lets businesses fund a job without paying the freelancer upfront.
paragraphs: Tunisie Freelance, a Tunisian platform for hiring freelancers, holds a client’s payment until the business approves the completed work. Companies post a mission and budget for free, review proposals and portfolios, then deposit the fee by bank card, PayPal or Apple Pay.

Founder Slim Skhab said the arrangement is designed to prevent clients losing an advance when work is not delivered. The platform releases the money after approval; clients can open a dispute or request cancellation. Freelancers pay a commission of about 10%, while clients pay none.

As of 20 novembre 2026, the platform listed more than 23 000 freelancer profiles and had hosted more than 1 200 missions. It is available in French, Arabic and English on web and mobile, and overseas businesses, including diaspora companies, can set budgets in euros or dollars.

tn.headline: Tunisia’s SECADENORD develops AI tool to cut pumping costs
tn.dek: Aqua Min 360 analyses water volumes and electricity use, recommending lower-tariff pumping periods and the most efficient pumps.
paragraphs: Tunisia’s Société d’exploitation du canal et des adductions des eaux du Nord (SECADENORD) has developed Aqua Min 360, an artificial-intelligence application to manage water resources and reduce electricity use at its pumping stations. The tool was examined at a working session chaired by Agriculture Minister Ezzeddine Ben Cheikh on Monday.

The application continuously analyses pumped-water volumes and electricity consumption, then recommends when to pump, how many pumps to operate and which equipment performs best. It also tracks water quality, pump condition and availability. SECADENORD’s stations at Sidi El Barrak, Tarf, Fondouk Jedid and Béjaoua are among the company’s most energy-intensive facilities.

Aqua Min 360 uses a national artificial-intelligence model to identify lower-priced electricity periods, including at night. Participants said its development should continue and its use be extended to the relevant administrations and technical bodies.

tn.headline: Tunis science centre schedules eighth aviation day for 24 December
tn.dek: The public event will feature aviation professionals, flight simulators and activities aimed especially at young people.
paragraphs: The Cité des Sciences à Tunis, a science centre, will hold its eighth Aviation Day on 24 December under the theme “Les Ailes de la Cité’26”. The event is open to the public, with particular attention to young people.

The centre is organising the programme with Tunisia’s defence and interior ministries, the Centre of Excellence in Aeronautical Industry Trades and the Tunisian Aeronautics Association, alongside other institutions and businesses. Organisers have scheduled discussions led by aviation professionals, exhibitions, a documentary on the history of aviation in Tunisia, competitions and flight-simulator sessions.

The event is also being held in connection with International Civil Aviation Day, which falls on 7 December. The organisers say the programme is intended to introduce young people to aviation careers and technology.

zm.dek: The proposed line from Chingola to Luacano has partial African Development Bank funding, but its economic case remains the question.
paragraphs: The Zambia-Lobito Railway project, a proposed link between Chingola in Zambia and Luacano in Angola, has named preferred bidders for engineering, procurement and construction contracts. zm.headline: Lusaka court orders Kang’ombe to pay K100,000 over Mpundu’s absence
zm.dek: The former lawmaker has five days to pay the bond after failing to explain why Mpundu, facing a seditious-practices charge, missed court.
paragraphs: A Lusaka magistrate’s court ordered Christopher Kang’ombe, a former Kamfinsa member of parliament, to pay K100,000 after he failed to account for the whereabouts of Binwell Mpundu, a former Nkana lawmaker. Magistrate Webster Milumbe gave him five days to pay.

Kang’ombe was one of Mpundu’s sureties and had to explain the accused’s continued absence from court. If he does not pay, a warrant of distress will be executed against him. Mpundu faces a charge of seditious practices.

Another surety, former Chilubi lawmaker Mulenga Fube, paid K100,000 on November 3 after failing to account for Mpundu’s location. Mpundu has been missing since August, and the court has issued a bench warrant. He is accused of making social-media statements on December 20, 2024, allegedly encouraging opposition members to arm themselves.

Lalliot, who arrived in Morocco in May, completed the visit after the signing. The report identifies the recipient only as a local company and does not name it.

The financing comes amid recent French investment in Western Sahara, in line with France's 2024 position in favour of Moroccan sovereignty over the territory.

ls.headline: Berea health team vaccinates 84% of St Theresa target children
ls.dek: The week-long measles drive followed four confirmed cases and included contact tracing for children aged nine months to 15 years.
paragraphs: Health workers in Berea vaccinated 84% of the target children in the St Theresa catchment during a campaign run from Monday to Friday. The District Health Management Team (DHMT) began the drive after four confirmed measles cases prompted a public-health alert.

District Child Health Officer Malehano Ramatutu said some parents refused vaccination. Children with possible measles symptoms were not vaccinated and remain under close monitoring. The DHMT did not publish the target population’s total, so the 84% is not a district-wide coverage rate.

The latest outbreak figures cited by the DHMT were dated 16 November and pre-date the campaign result: they recorded 19 confirmed cases in Berea, 345 in Leribe and 69 in Botha-Bothe. At that point, 395 people had recovered, with no deaths or hospital admissions recorded.
